findings.body: csv_rows, csv_escape, dump_streaming, dump_pretty, margins_for, and usable_width all contain real logic (column ordering, quoting rules, chunking, margin arithmetic) but none are covered by any test in this diff. The repo does have a test for csv_header, showing exporter functions are expected to be tested; a bug in any of these (e.g. off-by-one in chunking, wrong quote escaping, incorrect margin math) would currently pass unnoticed.

findings.title: Test cannot meaningfully fail: no controlled 'now', trivial assertion
findings.body:
Unlike test_token_expires_after_an_hour, which passes an explicit `now=` to freeze the expiry check at a specific point, this new test calls `is_expired(token.expires_at)` with no `now` argument and checks it immediately after issuing a token. Since the token was just issued, it will always be far from expiry regardless of whether the expiry-window logic is correct — the assertion cannot catch a real boundary bug (e.g. an off-by-one in the expiry window). The `token.issued_at.date() == datetime.now(timezone.utc).date()` check is similarly not exercising the 'still valid inside the expiry window' behaviour the PR claims to test; it only checks issuance timestamp, and is itself vulnerable to flaking around UTC midnight since two separate `datetime.now()` calls are compared.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Test compares two separately-sampled clocks; flaky at UTC midnight

findings.title: `is_expired` called without `now=` and with a different argument than the sibling test
findings.body: The only other call to `is_expired` in this file (line 6) passes `now=` explicitly and passes a timestamp derived from the issue time. Line 12 passes `token.expires_at` with no `now`, so it depends on (a) `now` having a default that reads the real clock and (b) the first positional parameter meaning "expiry instant" rather than "issued instant". If either assumption is wrong the test raises `TypeError` or asserts the opposite of what it reads. Please confirm the signature and pass `now=` explicitly for consistency with line 6.

findings.title: No test covers coupon expiry rejection
findings.body:
apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon expiring tomorrow, so it never exercises this branch. If the comparison logic were inverted, off-by-one, or the exception were never raised, no test would fail.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ New CouponExpired branch has no test

findings.title: Expiry check breaks on missing, null or naive expires_at
findings.body: `coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` imposes three new requirements on every coupon object reaching `apply_coupon`: the attribute must exist, it must not be `None`, and it must be timezone-aware. Any coupon lacking the attribute raises `AttributeError`; `None` or a naive datetime raises `TypeError` ("can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes") — both surface as a 500-style crash rather than the intended `CouponExpired`. The fact that the existing test had to be amended to pass `expires_at=tomorrow()` is direct evidence that coupons were previously constructed without it, so other construction sites and persisted rows may also lack it. Guard the branch, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and coupon.expires_at < now`, and normalise naive values to UTC before comparing.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async function stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is declared `async` but contains no `await`; the HTTP call is made with the synchronous `requests` library. When awaited from the request handler, the coroutine runs on the event loop thread and `requests.get` blocks it for the full duration of the call — up to the configured 5 second timeout — freezing every other in-flight request in the same worker. This is exactly the failure mode the existing `fetch_plan` above avoids by taking an `httpx.AsyncClient` and awaiting `client.get`.

Fix by following the module's existing pattern: accept (or create) an `httpx.AsyncClient` and `await client.get("https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}", timeout=5)`. If the sync library must be kept, wrap it with `anyio.to_thread.run_sync` / `loop.run_in_executor` so it does not run on the loop thread, and drop the misleading `async` otherwise.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Async function name masks blocking I/O call

findings.title: No test covers fetch_plan_limits or its blocking I/O behaviour
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is a new async function that performs a synchronous, blocking network call (requests.get) inside an async def — the core defect this PR's title warns about. There is no test in the diff that exercises this function, so nothing would fail if the function were changed to be correctly async, changed to return wrong data, or if the blocking call caused event-loop stalls under concurrent load. A test using a mocked event loop (e.g. asserting the coroutine yields control, or that no blocking call occurs during await) or even a basic unit test asserting correct return value from a mocked response is absent.

findings.title: tenant_id interpolated unescaped into internal billing URL
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}`. `requests` does not remove dot-segments or percent-encode path characters for you, so a `tenant_id` such as `../../admin/keys` or `1?admin=1` reaches `billing.internal` as a different path/query than intended. Because the target is an internal, likely unauthenticated service, this turns a tenant identifier into a limited server-side request forgery primitive against the billing host.

Fix: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. UUID or integer) before use, or at minimum pass it through `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe='')`. The same treatment should be applied to the pre-existing `fetch_plan` on line 6.

findings.title: Bare `except` swallows KeyboardInterrupt/SystemExit and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, including `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit`. If a shutdown signal or a task cancellation arrives while `_client.send` is in flight, this handler absorbs it and returns `None`, so the process appears to continue normally and the shutdown/cancel is lost. Narrow it to `except Exception:`.

Separately, the body does nothing but `return None`. The PR description says "catch and log, then continue", but there is no log call — every push failure (auth error, malformed payload, permanent endpoint outage) becomes indistinguishable from success, and nobody will notice metrics have stopped flowing. Add a `logger.warning(...)`/`logger.exception(...)` before returning.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Metrics push failures swallowed silently, no log despite PR intent

findings.title: No test covers the new catch-and-continue behavior
findings.body: The change to push_metrics now swallows exceptions from _client.send and returns None instead of propagating. There is no accompanying test verifying that (a) a successful send still returns the client's result, and (b) an exception from _client.send is caught and results in None rather than propagating. If this logic were reverted or broken (e.g., re-raising, or catching only specific exceptions and behaving differently), nothing in the repository would fail to signal it.

findings.title: try_consume checks and updates the counter without holding _lock
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` on line 15, then awaits on line 18 (an explicit suspension point), then writes `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` on line 19 — all outside `_lock`, which every other mutation of `_counters` (line 9) holds.

Two concrete consequences:

1. **Limit bypass.** N coroutines can each read the same `current`, each pass the `current + cost > LIMIT` check, and each admit its cost. With the counter near the limit, the effective total admitted is up to N*cost over LIMIT — exactly the noisy-client starvation this change is meant to prevent.
2. **Lost updates.** The write is an absolute assignment of a value captured *before* the await, not an increment. Any `consume()` call that commits while `try_consume` is suspended is overwritten and its cost vanishes from the tally.

Fix: take the same lock and re-read inside it, e.g.

```python
async def try_consume(tenant, cost):
    async with _lock:
        current = _counters.get(tenant, 0)
        if current + cost > LIMIT:
            return False
        _counters[tenant] = current + cost
        return True
```

and drop the `await asyncio.sleep(0)`, or move it outside the critical section if it exists for fairness reasons.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rate limit bypassable: check-then-act outside the lock in try_consume

findings.title: No test exercises try_consume's concurrent/race behaviour
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters (line 15), awaits (line 18), then writes (line 19) without acquiring _lock, unlike consume which uses the lock throughout. This is a classic check-then-act race: concurrent callers can both pass the limit check before either writes, allowing the tenant to exceed LIMIT. No test file is present in this diff, so nothing currently would catch this race — a sequential/single-call test would pass even though the function is unsafe under concurrency, and no test verifies that LIMIT is actually enforced when calls overlap.

findings.title: try_consume has non-atomic race condition not documented
findings.body: The function `try_consume` reads `_counters[tenant]` on line 15, checks it against LIMIT on line 16, sleeps on line 18, then updates the counter on line 19. This is non-atomic: between the check and the write, another coroutine could have already incremented the counter via `consume()`, causing the limit to be exceeded. A caller expecting atomicity based on the function name would be wrong. This needs to be documented.

findings.title: Public constant LIMIT lacks explanation
findings.body: The constant `LIMIT = 1000` is exported at module level but its meaning is not documented. Callers need to know this is a per-tenant rate limit threshold and what its unit is (requests? bytes? operations?).

findings.title: Return shape change breaks tuple-unpacking caller in reports/weekly.py
findings.body:
`lookup_user` now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}` instead of `(name, email)`. The existing caller `render_row` in reports/weekly.py does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`; iterating a 3-key dict yields three keys, so this raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call. Even if the dict had exactly two keys, the caller would bind key strings rather than values, silently producing `"name <email>"`.

Either update `render_row` to `user = lookup_user(user_id); return f"{user['name']} <{user['email']}>"`, or keep the tuple contract and add a separate function/`NamedTuple` so existing unpacking callers keep working.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Return-shape change breaks existing caller, untested

findings.title: Stale docstring: documents old return type
findings.body:
The docstring states `Return (name, email) for a user.` but the function now returns a dict with keys name, email, and tier. This will cause callers consulting the docstring to expect a tuple and unpack it incorrectly, as evidenced by the existing caller in reports/weekly.py which unpacks the return value as `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Updating the docstring to match the new dict return type is essential.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still documents the old (name, email) tuple return

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil after a failed INSERT
findings.body:
The error from `db.Exec` is bound inside the `if` statement's scope on line 15 and only logged. Lines 18-19 then declare a brand-new `var err error` (always nil) and return it, so `WriteSettlement` reports success for every failed settlement insert. Callers that check `if err := WriteSettlement(...); err != nil` will never see a write failure, and a settlement row can silently go missing from the end-of-day batch.

If the intent really is "log and continue", make that explicit and return nothing meaningful from the error path only after a deliberate decision — but the dead `var err error` declaration strongly suggests the author meant to propagate. Suggested fix:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
    log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
    return err
}
return nil
```

Note also the inconsistency: validation failures on line 13 *are* propagated, so the function's contract already promises a non-nil error on failure.

findings.title: WriteSettlement returns error but swallows DB failures silently
findings.body: The function signature `func WriteSettlement(db *sql.DB, s Settlement) error` promises callers that it returns an error indicating success or failure. However, the implementation catches and logs the database insertion error on line 15-16 without returning it, then returns a nil error variable on line 19. This violates the return type contract: callers checking the error will believe the write succeeded when it actually failed. The name `Write*` suggests the write is being attempted and reported, but failures are silently swallowed. Either the function should return the DB error, or the name and signature should be changed to reflect that it logs-and-continues semantics (e.g., `WriteSettlementIgnoringErrors`).

findings.title: WriteSettlement has no test covering its error-return behavior
findings.body: WriteSettlement's return value on insert failure is `err`, a freshly declared variable that is always nil (line 18-19), regardless of whether the db.Exec on line 15 failed. There is no test file in this diff, so nothing exercises the failure path of WriteSettlement to confirm what it returns. A test that inserted with a failing db and asserted on the returned error would have caught this discrepancy between the intended 'log and continue' semantics and the actual always-nil return.

findings.title: Mutable default argument accumulates state across calls
findings.body:
`attempted=[]` is evaluated once at function-definition time, so every call that omits the argument shares the same list object. Line 10 appends to it and line 11 returns it, meaning the second call returns its own failures plus every failure from the first call, and so on for the process lifetime. Callers that treat the return value as "recipients that failed in this batch" will get monotonically growing, incorrect results, and the list keeps the recipient objects alive indefinitely.

Fix with the standard sentinel: `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` then `attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Mutable default arg leaks recipients across calls and grows unbounded

findings.title: Public function has no docstring; mutable default arg behavior unclear
findings.body: The function `send_with_retries` is publicly exported but lacks a docstring. More critically, it uses a mutable default argument (`attempted=[]`), whose behavior is non-obvious to callers: the list is shared across calls and accumulates state. A caller who is unaware of this would expect a fresh list on each invocation, leading to incorrect results. A docstring explaining this contract is necessary.

findings.title: No test exercises send_with_retries, including the mutable-default bug
findings.body: send_with_retries uses a mutable default argument (attempted=[]) which will accumulate entries across multiple calls that don't pass their own list. There is no test in this diff exercising this function at all, so this bug (and the retry/return behaviour in general) is completely uncovered — a regression or the existing defect would not be caught by any existing suite.

findings.title: compute_rounding silently changes >= 0.5 to > 0.5
findings.body:
This PR is described as a pure rename, but `calc_rounding` used `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5` and `compute_rounding` uses `line.remainder_cents > 0.5`. For a remainder of exactly 0.5 the function now returns 0 where it previously returned 1, i.e. standard half-up rounding becomes round-down-on-tie. Exact .5 remainders are the common case when splitting cents evenly (e.g. a two-way split of an odd cent amount), so this is reachable and will shift invoice totals by one cent. Restore `>=`, or if the change is intentional, split it out of the rename with a test covering the 0.5 boundary.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Silent behavior change hidden in rename: >= became >

findings.title: Rounding logic change lacks documentation
findings.body: The `compute_rounding` function's comparison operator changed from `>=` to `>` on line 41, which alters the rounding behavior for the boundary case where `remainder_cents == 0.5`. This is a functional change that should be documented in a comment or commit message explaining why the rounding threshold changed. Without this explanation, future maintainers may not understand the intent or may inadvertently revert it.

findings.title: Module docstring uses outdated terminology
findings.body: The module docstring refers to 'Line-item calculators' but the functions have been renamed from `calc_*` to `compute_*`. While this is a minor semantic distinction, the docstring should be updated to reflect the new naming convention and intent. Consider updating to 'Line-item computers' or 'Line-item computation functions' to match the new API naming.

findings.title: page_of_sorted violates pagination contract via off-by-one slice
findings.body:
The function `page_of_sorted` slices with `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` on line 12, returning one fewer record than `page_of` does. This creates inconsistent pagination behavior: `page_of` returns `PAGE_SIZE` records per page, but `page_of_sorted` returns `PAGE_SIZE - 1`. findings.title: AttributeError when purchase_order is None (the common case)
findings.body:
`invoice.purchase_order` is typed `str | None` and is documented as only set for customers on invoicing terms ("roughly one account in twenty"). The removed guard was not redundant — the type is optional, not non-null. With the guard gone, `invoice.purchase_order.upper()` raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` for the ~95% of invoices with no purchase order, which will break rendering in production.

Restore the conditional append, e.g.:

```python
def header_lines(invoice):
    lines = [f"Invoice {invoice.number}"]
    if invoice.purchase_order is not None:
        lines.append(f"PO {invoice.purchase_order.upper()}")
    return lines
```

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`billing.gateway.charge` is documented as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." Decorating `charge_card` with `@retry(attempts=3)` means any transient failure that occurs *after* the gateway has created the charge (timeout on the response, 502 from a proxy, connection reset) will be retried and create a second and third charge. The customer is billed up to 3x and the extra charges are invisible to this code because only the last return value survives.

The gateway already provides the correct mechanism: the docstring notes it supports an `Idempotency-Key` header. Either (a) generate a key per logical charge attempt in the caller and pass it through `charge(...)` so retries collapse server-side, then keep the retry; or (b) drop the retry from this path entirely and let the caller reconcile via `fetch_charge`. Retrying `get_charge` (line 6-7) is fine — that one is documented safe to repeat — so the fix is specific to the new function.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wrapper on non-idempotent charge can double-bill customers

findings.title: Non-idempotent function wrapped with retry, no contract documented
findings.body: The new `charge_card` function retries calls to `charge`, which the underlying gateway function explicitly documents as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." A caller using `charge_card` would reasonably expect retries to be safe, but they are not—each retry attempt creates a new charge unless an Idempotency-Key is passed to the gateway. The function needs a docstring that either (1) documents this hazard and directs the caller to provide an Idempotency-Key, or (2) implements the safety itself by generating and passing such a key.

findings.title: No test would catch duplicate charges from retrying a non-idempotent call
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge, which is documented as NOT idempotent (each call creates a new charge), with @retry(attempts=3) and no idempotency key. There is no test in this diff verifying retry behavior for charge_card at all, so a bug where a transient failure causes 2-3 real charges to be created would currently pass silently — nothing exercises this function to assert it only issues one underlying charge attempt (or fails loudly) under retry.

findings.title: Naive/aware datetime subtraction raises TypeError in expires_within
findings.body:
`datetime.now()` returns a naive local-time datetime, but `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so `expires_within` fails for every invite, not just an edge case. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does; that also removes the silent local-vs-UTC offset error that would remain even if both sides were naive. The `.replace(microsecond=0)` truncation is harmless but serves no purpose here.

findings.title: Referer no longer scrubbed: auth token written to logs on 5xx
findings.body:
The previous code special-cased `Referer` and passed it through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before adding it to the dict that is serialised on line 6. The new single-line assignment copies the raw header value. `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py` builds notebook URLs as `f"{base}?token={token}"`, so the browser attaches that token in the `Referer` of every subresource request; any 5xx triggers `log_method(json.dumps(headers, ...))` and persists a usable credential into the log stream, where it is readable by anyone with log access and typically survives in aggregation/backup systems.

Restore the per-header scrub for `Referer` (and consider applying it to any other header that can carry a URI). If the goal was just to simplify, keep the branch: `headers[header] = _scrub_uri(v, extra_param_keys) if header == "Referer" else v`.

Secondary consequence: with the only call site removed, `extra_param_keys` is now unused in this function, which is a signal the removal was accidental rather than intentional.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Referer no longer scrubbed: auth token written to logs on 5xx

findings.title: Logging code now exposes auth tokens without warning
findings.body: The code at line 5 logs request headers including Referer directly without scrubbing. According to `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py`, the Referer header intentionally carries auth tokens as query parameters on every subresource request. The removed `_scrub_uri()` call was protecting against logging these tokens. This change now leaks tokens into logs. Either the change should be reverted, or a clear comment must document that tokens in Referer headers are being logged intentionally and the risks are understood.

findings.title: Removal of Referer token scrubbing has no test guarding it
findings.body: The change deletes the call to _scrub_uri for the Referer header, restoring raw header values (including any embedded auth token, per token_authenticated_url) into logs. No test file is included in this diff, and none is evident in the repository context that asserts scrubbed vs. raw Referer values in the logged JSON. If this regresses again, or is reverted incorrectly, nothing would fail. Add a test that sets a Referer header containing a token-bearing URL and asserts the logged output has the token scrubbed.

findings.title: xlinkhref no longer validated, allowing javascript: URLs through
findings.body:
The PR describes this as trimming an attribute allowlist, but this branch is not an allowlist — it is the URL-scheme guard. Previously `xlinkhref` was routed into `isAnchorLinkAllowed(value)`, which rejects the `javascript:`, `data:text/html` and `vbscript:` prefixes. With `xlinkhref` removed from the condition, that attribute no longer matches any URL check and falls through to whatever the function's default/permissive tail returns, so `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:...">` in author markdown reaches the DOM unfiltered. SVG `xlink:href` is a navigable URL sink in browsers exactly like `href`, so this is a live XSS path, not a cosmetic cleanup.

If the genuine intent is to stop rendering `xlink:href` at all, the attribute must be dropped from the rendered-attribute allowlist elsewhere; removing it from the validation branch achieves the opposite. Otherwise restore `|| attribute === 'xlinkhref'`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Dropping xlinkhref from URL check re-enables SVG javascript: XSS

findings.title: Removal of xlinkhref check from validateProp has no test coverage shown
findings.body: The condition that previously routed the 'xlinkhref' attribute through isAnchorLinkAllowed has been removed, meaning xlinkhref attributes (used for SVG xlink:href, which can carry javascript:/data: URLs) will now fall through to whatever default handling exists below this branch. No test file is included in this diff to confirm what the new behavior is for xlinkhref values, e.g. that a malicious xlink:href is still rejected by a later branch, or that legitimate uses still render correctly. If the removal is wrong (e.g., no other branch validates this attribute), nothing in the current test suite is shown to catch it.

findings.title: Removing ValidateID lets unvalidated project names reach buildPath
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the request query string and, after this change, is no longer checked by `common.ValidateID` before being used as the project scope for the list operation. The file DAO's `buildPath` documents that it performs no validation of its own and that "callers are required to have validated the names before this point"; `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)` cleans `..` segments, so a value such as `../../other` resolves to a path outside the intended project folder rather than being rejected. The PR description's premise that "the path join already scopes under the folder root" is incorrect — `filepath.Join` normalises traversal, it does not confine it.

Beyond traversal, the check also guaranteed the parameter was a well-formed identifier for every other backend (e.g. as a datastore key or filter value); downstream code may now receive names it never expected. Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` call inside the `len(projectQueryParameter) > 0` branch, before the path/query comparison on line 4.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removed ValidateID lets project query param traverse paths

findings.title: Removed ValidateID check on projectQueryParameter has no test guarding behavior
findings.body: The diff removes the call to common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) and its error path, relying instead on filepath.Join scoping in buildPath. No test in this diff (or referenced) exercises list() with a malicious or malformed projectQueryParameter (e.g. containing '..' or path separators) to confirm the new behavior is safe and equivalent. If the assumption that buildPath's Join fully mitigates unvalidated input is wrong, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: Buffer pre-reserved from unvalidated client Content-Length
findings.body:
`Reserve(contentLength)` commits memory based on a value that comes straight off the wire, before a single byte of `body` has been read or validated. A client can send `Content-Length: 5000000000` with a few bytes of body and the server will attempt the reservation anyway; the `io.Copy` on line 8 will then return a small `n`, but the allocation has already happened. Repeating this across concurrent part uploads exhausts memory even though no real data was transferred.

The previous code grew the RW incrementally as bytes actually arrived, so the resident size was bounded by what the client really sent. If the pre-reservation is worth keeping for the MD5 pass, clamp it — e.g. `Reserve(min(contentLength, maxPartSize))` with the S3 per-part ceiling, and only when `contentLength > 0` — so the declared length can shrink the number of grow steps but never inflate the footprint beyond what a legitimate part could be.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Buffer pre-reserved from unvalidated client Content-Length

findings.title: No test covers pre-reservation behavior with attacker-controlled length
findings.body: The change now eagerly reserves memory sized by the caller-supplied contentLength before any bytes are read (`multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength)`). There is no test in this diff that verifies behavior when contentLength is large, zero, negative, or mismatched with the actual body size. If Reserve mishandles such inputs (e.g. allocating excessive memory or panicking on a negative value), nothing in the existing test suite would fail, since no test was added or shown to exercise this path.

findings.title: Default S3 scheme flipped from https to plaintext http
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only downgraded to plaintext when a caller explicitly set `is_secure=False`; every other case — including the overwhelmingly common case where `is_secure` is not present in `request.meta` at all and `.get()` returns `None` — produced `https`.

The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats `None` (unset), `0`, and `""` as "not secure", so any request that does not explicitly opt in now travels over plaintext `http` to `{bucket}.s3.amazonaws.com`, exposing request paths, query strings and AWS credentials/signatures carried in the request to network observers and tampering.

These two expressions are only equivalent when the key is always present and always a real bool, which is not guaranteed by `dict.get`. Restore the secure-by-default semantics, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or make it explicit with `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)`.

findings.title: S3 downloader now defaults to plaintext HTTP when is_secure is unset
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` was a secure-by-default three-state check: only an explicit `is_secure=False` produced `http`; missing key (`None`) produced `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` is a two-state truthiness check, so `None` (key absent \u2014 the normal case for any request that does not opt in) and any other falsy value now yield `http`.

Consequence: the URL built on line 6 is `http://<bucket>.s3.amazonaws.com/...` for every S3 request that does not explicitly set the meta key. S3 requests carry AWS SigV4 `Authorization`/`x-amz-*` headers (or presigned query parameters), and the fetched object body is likewise sent in the clear. A network-position attacker can read the signature material and object contents, and can tamper with responses, since there is no TLS to authenticate the endpoint either.

Restore the secure default, e.g.:

```python
scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"
```

or, if the ternary must be simplified, `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"`.

findings.title: Default scheme change to http has no test coverage shown
findings.body: The change alters default behavior: previously, when 'is_secure' was absent/None, the scheme defaulted to 'https'; now it defaults to 'http'. No test in this diff verifies the scheme selected for the absent-key case, the True case, or the False case. If this default flip were wrong (e.g., unintentionally exposing requests over plaintext HTTP by default), nothing in the visible change would catch it.

findings.title: DELETE now authorises as "push", dropping the delete action entirely
findings.body:
The old switch had an explicit `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"`. The new condition only special-cases GET and HEAD, so `DELETE` falls into the `else` branch and is checked against the `push` permission. Any account configured with push-but-not-delete can now destroy tags/manifests, and accounts holding only `delete` will be rejected. The `delete` action becomes unreachable, so every ACL entry granting it is dead configuration. Restore an explicit DELETE branch that sets `action = "delete"`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorizes as "push", bypassing the delete permission

findings.title: Default for unlisted methods changed from "pull" to "push"

The new inverted test sends all of them to `push`, so requests that previously succeeded for a pull-only principal — notably CORS preflight `OPTIONS` — will now be denied. If the stricter default is intentional, it should be stated; otherwise enumerate the write methods explicitly rather than negating the read methods.

findings.title: No test covers DELETE now mapping to push instead of delete

findings.title: Size-limit eviction clears the whole shared cache, including the new entry
findings.body:
When the cache crosses 1000 entries, `_CACHE.clear()` drops every tenant, not just the oldest one. Two consequences: (a) the entry written on line 10 is immediately discarded, so a `get_tenant_fresh` call that trips the threshold leaves nothing cached for the tenant it just fetched; (b) every other caller of `get_tenant` (line 5) starts getting `None` for tenants that were warm a moment ago, producing a stampede of misses against whatever backs `_fetch`. If a bound is needed, evict a single entry (e.g. `_CACHE.pop(next(iter(_CACHE)))`) or use an LRU structure such as `collections.OrderedDict`/`functools.lru_cache` rather than flushing the shared map.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Attacker-chosen tenant_id can flush the whole shared cache

findings.title: get_tenant_fresh has no test coverage

If the eviction threshold logic were wrong (e.g. off-by-one, or clearing on every call), or if _fetch's result were stored incorrectly, nothing would fail. Add a test that calls get_tenant_fresh, asserts the returned value matches the fetched tenant, asserts the cache was updated, and exercises the eviction path (populate _CACHE past the threshold and confirm it clears).

findings.title: verify/cert accepted by request() but never applied to the send path
findings.body:
The new `request()` signature still takes `verify=None` and `cert=None` (lines 148-149), but the body only copies method, url, headers, files, data, params, auth, cookies, allow_redirects, proxies and hooks onto `req`. `verify` and `cert` are never assigned to the request, never merged with any session-level default, and `self.send(prep)` on line 167 is called with no extra arguments, so `HTTPAdapter.send(request)` (line 366) receives no verification settings at all.

Entry point: any caller of `session.request(..., verify='/path/to/ca.pem')` or `verify=True`, including all of `get`/`post`/etc. Sink: the TLS handshake performed inside the adapter. A caller who explicitly pins a CA bundle or client certificate gets a connection that ignores both, and if the adapter's own default is permissive the result is an unauthenticated TLS connection that any on-path attacker can intercept.

Either thread `verify`/`cert` onto the prepared request and pass them through to `adapter.send()`, or fail loudly (drop the parameters from the signature) until the plumbing exists, so that callers cannot believe a verification setting is in effect when it is not.

findings.title: A new HTTPAdapter (and connection pool) is constructed on every send
findings.body:
`send()` instantiates `HTTPAdapter()` per call, so each request builds a fresh `PoolManager` that is discarded afterwards. That removes the connection reuse the `Session` exists to provide and leaks sockets until GC closes them (keep-alive connections in a dropped pool are not closed deterministically). The adapter should be created once (e.g. in `__init__`, mounted per-prefix) and reused, with `close()` clearing it.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ New HTTPAdapter per send plus no-op close() drops connection reuse

findings.title: `_send_request` deleted but `old_request` still calls it
findings.body: `_send_request` is removed in this diff, yet the surviving `old_request` path still ends with `return self._send_request(r, **args)`. Any call into `old_request` now raises `AttributeError: 'Session' object has no attribute '_send_request'`. Either keep the helper until `old_request` is deleted, or inline the two lines (`r.send(prefetch=...)`; `return r.response`) at the call site.

findings.title: New `request()` silently discards timeout/verify/cert/prefetch and all session state
findings.body: The rewritten `request()` accepts `timeout`, `verify`, `cert`, `prefetch`, `config` and `return_response` but never uses them — they are not copied onto `req` and not forwarded to `send()`. Existing callers (including `get`/`post`/... which forward `**kwargs`) will keep passing `verify=False`, `cert=(...)`, `timeout=5` and get behaviour that silently ignores them; `verify` in particular changes TLS trust decisions without any error. The method also no longer merges session-level `self.headers`, `self.params`, `self.auth`, `self.cookies`, `self.hooks` or `self.config` into the request, so a configured `Session` now behaves like a bare one. Either thread these through to `prepare()`/`send()` or raise on the ones not yet supported rather than dropping them.

findings.title: `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` is not a package-relative import
findings.body: Every other intra-package import in this module is relative (`from .utils import ...`, `from .packages.urllib3.poolmanager import ...`). `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` only resolves under Python 2 implicit relative imports; under Python 3 (or with `absolute_import` in effect) it raises `ImportError` at module import time, breaking the whole library. Use `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: close() now a no-op with no test asserting connection cleanup
findings.body: Session.close() previously cleared the poolmanager to release pooled connections; it is now `pass`, silently dropping that behaviour. If any existing test verified that close() actually released resources (e.g. checking poolmanager state or socket closure), it would now be exercising dead code, and if no such test exists, this resource-cleanup regression is completely uncovered.

findings.title: Session.send() reroute to HTTPAdapter lacks visible test coverage
findings.body: send() no longer calls request.send() directly but constructs a fresh HTTPAdapter() per call and delegates to it. This is a significant behavioural change (new object per send, different code path for actually performing I/O) that isn't exercised by any test in this diff. If HTTPAdapter.send() has different semantics (e.g. around prefetch, proxies, or connection reuse) than PreparedRequest.send(), nothing here would catch a regression.

findings.title: Stale docstring for close() method
findings.body: The `close()` method previously had a docstring stating it disposes of internal state by closing the PoolManager and its pooled connections. This docstring was removed when the method body was changed to `pass`, but the removal happened implicitly through the deletion of the entire docstring block. However, the documented behavior (closing pooled connections) no longer occurs. If the docstring were to remain, it would be actively misleading about what the method does. The current state (no docstring) is acceptable, but this documents the contract change: callers relying on close() to clean up connections will find it no longer does so.

findings.title: `close()` is now a no-op, so `with Session()` no longer releases connections
findings.body: `close()` previously cleared the PoolManager; it is now `pass`, while `__exit__` (line 129) still calls it. Code relying on `with requests.session() as s:` or an explicit `s.close()` to release pooled sockets will silently leak them. Once the adapter is owned by the session, `close()` should close/clear it. Related: `self.poolmanager` and the `init_poolmanager()` override hook are removed without replacement — subclasses that override `init_poolmanager` to customise pool size or SSL settings will silently stop having any effect.

findings.title: send() method documentation does not describe HTTPAdapter delegation
findings.body: The `send()` method's docstring is minimal ("Send a given PreparedRequest.") but the implementation now delegates to an HTTPAdapter. The docstring does not explain this architectural change or that the adapter is created per-call. For a public method, callers may want to know whether HTTPAdapter instances are reused or created fresh, and how exceptions from the adapter are handled. Consider expanding the docstring to document the adapter pattern, or accept the current terse style if that is the house convention.

findings.title: Malformed Cookie header makes `cookies` return None, breaking callers
findings.body:
In the new `HTTPRequest.cookies`, a parse failure sets `self._cookies = None` and the property then returns `None`. Every caller treats the result as a mapping: `get_cookie` does `if name in self.request.cookies` (web.py:321), which raises `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable`, and `clear_all_cookies` does `self.request.cookies.iterkeys()` (web.py:367), which raises `AttributeError`. Because `hasattr(self, "_cookies")` is then True, the `None` is cached for the lifetime of the request, so every subsequent access fails too. A client-supplied malformed `Cookie` header is enough to trigger it, i.e. a remotely reachable 500.

The old code never returned a non-mapping: on failure it kept the (possibly partially loaded) `SimpleCookie` and called `self.clear_all_cookies()`. At request level the equivalent safe behaviour is `self._cookies = Cookie.SimpleCookie()` (an empty mapping) in the `except` branch, leaving the response-side clearing to `RequestHandler`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header makes request.cookies None, crashing all cookie readers

findings.title: RequestHandler.cookies removed with no delegating alias
findings.body:
`RequestHandler.cookies` was a public, documented property; removing it outright breaks any application handler or third-party subclass that reads `self.cookies` (and any template doing `handler.cookies`). The mechanical fix is to keep a thin delegating property on `RequestHandler`:

```python
@property
def cookies(self):
    return self.request.cookies
```

That preserves the existing contract while still making the data available on `HTTPRequest`.

findings.title: Moved cookies property and its changed error path are untested
findings.body: The cookies property was moved from RequestHandler to HTTPRequest, and its exception handling behavior changed subtly: previously on a parse failure the handler called self.clear_all_cookies(); now on failure self._cookies is simply set to None (httpserver.py line 523), which will break get_cookie/clear_all_cookies (web.py lines 321-322, 367) with an AttributeError/TypeError when a malformed Cookie header is sent. No test exercises get_cookie, clear_all_cookies, or a malformed Cookie header, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: Incomplete docstring: cookies property can return None
findings.body: The `cookies` property on HTTPRequest has a docstring that states it returns "A dictionary of Cookie.Morsel objects", but the code at line 523 explicitly sets `self._cookies = None` when parsing fails. This means callers cannot rely on receiving a dictionary in all cases. The docstring should document this exception, or the behavior should be clarified for callers who will use this property directly (now that it has moved from RequestHandler to HTTPRequest, where callers are more likely to be unfamiliar with the implementation details).

findings.title: Boundary parameter never matches: whitespace not stripped after split(";")
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` keeps the optional linear whitespace that RFC 2616 allows (and that every browser emits) between parameters, so for the ubiquitous header `multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz` the second token is `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXyz"` and `k` becomes `" boundary"`. The comparison `k == "boundary"` is therefore False, the loop never breaks, and control falls into the `for ... else` branch which logs "Invalid multipart/form-data" — all multipart bodies are silently dropped. The previous code (`'boundary=' in content_type`) was immune to this. Strip the token before partitioning, e.g. `k, sep, v = field.strip().partition("=")`, and compare case-insensitively (`k.lower() == "boundary"`) since parameter names are case-insensitive.

findings.title: Content-Type parameters not stripped; boundary never matches
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` yields parameters with the leading space that RFC 2045/7231 producers conventionally emit, e.g. `multipart/form-data; boundary=----abc` splits into `["multipart/form-data", " boundary=----abc"]`. `field.partition("=")` then gives `k == " boundary"`, which never equals `"boundary"`, so the loop falls through to the `else` and logs "Invalid multipart/form-data" for essentially every real multipart request — the body is silently discarded instead of parsed. Use `field.strip().partition("=")` (and consider stripping surrounding double quotes from `v`, since `boundary="----abc"` is legal and would otherwise be passed to `_parse_mime_body` with the quotes attached).

Security note: the entry point is the client-supplied `Content-Type` request header and the sink is `_parse_mime_body(v, data)`. That flow is unchanged by this diff — the boundary was attacker-controlled before as well — so this is a correctness/availability defect for multipart clients rather than a new injection surface.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Quoted boundary value is passed through with its quotes

findings.title: No test exercises the new multi-field boundary parsing
findings.body: The change alters how the boundary parameter is extracted from Content-Type when 'boundary' is not the last field (e.g. 'multipart/form-data; charset=utf-8; boundary=xyz'). No test in this diff verifies that such a header is now parsed correctly, nor that the previous bug (boundary being non-last) is fixed. A regression back to the old split-based approach, or an off-by-one in the loop (e.g. not breaking correctly, or matching a wrong field named similarly), would not be caught by any existing test given none is present in this change.

findings.title: get_host ignores '?' and '#', allowing host-parsing confusion (SSRF)
findings.body:
`get_host` strips the scheme, then only treats `/` as the end of the authority before looking for `@` and `:`. Query and fragment delimiters are never considered, so the authority is over-read:

- `get_host('http://trusted.example.com?@evil.com/')` → after the scheme split `url == 'trusted.example.com?@evil.com/'`; the `/` split leaves `'trusted.example.com?@evil.com'`; the `@` split then discards everything before `@` as userinfo and returns host `evil.com`.
- `get_host('http://trusted.example.com#@evil.com/')` behaves identically.

`urllib.parse.urlsplit` returns `trusted.example.com` for both. Any caller that allowlists a URL with the stdlib parser (or any other RFC-3986 parser) and then lets urllib3 connect will connect to the attacker's host — a classic parser-differential SSRF / allowlist bypass. The same over-read also affects `:` port parsing, e.g. a `?`/`#` segment containing a colon.

Fix: terminate the authority at the first of `/`, `?`, or `#` (e.g. split on a small regex or delegate to `urlsplit`), and take the userinfo boundary as the *last* `@` within the authority only.

I can see the sink (this parser) but not the callers in this diff, so I cannot confirm an exploitable entry point in-repo; the rating assumes the usual `PoolManager.urlopen`/`connection_from_url` path where the URL originates from application input.

findings.title: No tests accompany newly added util.py helpers
findings.body: This PR introduces three functions (make_headers, get_host, is_connection_dropped) with real logic — header construction, URL parsing with error handling, and platform-specific connection-drop detection — but no test file is part of the diff. If any of these were subtly wrong (e.g. the LocationParseError message missing the actual value, or get_host mishandling an edge-case URL like IPv6 or missing scheme), nothing here would catch it.

findings.title: LocationParseError message never interpolates the URL
findings.body: The raised message is the literal string `"Failed to parse: %s"` — the `% url` (or `% port`) interpolation is missing, so every parse failure produces an identical, useless message with a dangling `%s`. Change to `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s" % url)`.

findings.title: is_connection_dropped falls off the end returning None
findings.body: The docstring promises a boolean, but the two code paths return different shapes: the `select` branch returns a list (`select(...)[0]`), and the `poll` branch returns `True` only from inside the loop — if `p.poll(0.0)` yields nothing, or yields fds that don't match, the function implicitly returns `None`. Any caller doing an identity/`is False` comparison, or asserting a bool in tests, will misbehave. Add an explicit `return False` after the loop and coerce the select branch with `bool(...)`.

findings.title: No test covers rejection of an invalid `direction` value
findings.body: The new validation `if sort not in SORTABLE or direction not in DIRECTIONS` has two independent failure branches. Only the `sort` branch is tested (test_rejects_an_unknown_sort_key). If the `direction not in DIRECTIONS` check were removed or broken (e.g. someone changes the condition to only check `sort`), no test would catch it, allowing an unvalidated `direction` string to reach the f-string interpolation on line 17.

findings.title: Return value for click events changed despite "types only" claim
findings.body: The old branch returned `click at ${x}`; the new case returns `click at ${x}, ${y}`. This is a behavioural change to the function's return value, not a type-level refactor, so any caller, log parser, snapshot test or UI string that consumes `describe()` output for click events now sees a different string. Either restore the original format or call out the output change explicitly (and update callers/snapshots).

findings.title: HTTPMove.location now a URL object, not the constructed string
findings.body:
Previously `self.location = location` stored exactly the value the caller passed (normally a `str`); only the header used the normalised `str(URL(location))`. After this change `self.location` is a `yarl.URL`.

This is an observable public-API change: `URL` does not support `str.startswith`, and `exc.location == "/login"` is False for `URL("/login")` in any code comparing against configured strings — exactly the usage the documentation describes. `URL` also normalises (percent-encoding, trailing-slash/path handling), so even `str(exc.location)` may not round-trip the original input.

If you only want to avoid constructing `URL` twice, keep the attribute as the original value:

```python
url = URL(location)
self.headers['Location'] = str(url)
self.location = location
```

If changing the attribute type is intentional, it needs a documentation update and a deprecation path.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ location attribute type change can silently break redirect allowlist checks

findings.title: HTTPMove.location now contradicts its documented type
findings.body: The documentation states that `HTTPMove.location` is "the string it was constructed with", but this change assigns a `URL` object instead. Callers expecting a string (as the docs promise) will break when they try string operations like `.startswith()` on the `URL` object, or will get unexpected behavior if they compare it directly against configured strings.

findings.title: No test verifies self.location remains a string after refactor
findings.body: self.location is now assigned URL(location) instead of the original string, which conflicts with the documented contract (docs/web_reference.rst) that location is 'the string it was constructed with' and is used with str.startswith by application code. No test in this diff (or apparently in the existing suite, since none is touched) asserts the type or string equality of self.location, so this behavior change would go undetected by CI.

findings.title: readany can return b'' before EOF after single wait
findings.body:
`_wait` documents that its future is also resolved at the end of a chunk, possibly with no new data in the buffer, and that "a caller must re-check its condition after waking rather than assuming data arrived." Replacing the `while` with an `if` removes exactly that re-check: after a spurious/end-of-chunk wake, control falls through to `self._read_nowait(-1)` with an empty buffer and `self._eof` still False, so `readany()` returns `b''`.

An empty return from `readany()` is the documented end-of-stream signal, so consumers looping `while True: chunk = await resp.content.readany(); if not chunk: break` will truncate the body silently. Restore the `while` loop so the buffer/EOF condition is re-evaluated after each wake.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Single-shot wait lets a peer force premature empty read (body truncation)

findings.title: No test covers spurious-wakeup behavior of readany after while->if change
findings.body: The docstring for _wait explicitly warns that the waiter can resolve 'at the end of a chunk' with no new data, so callers must re-check their condition after waking. Changing the loop `while not self._buffer and not self._eof` to a single `if` removes that re-check, meaning readany could return with an empty buffer despite not being at EOF if a spurious wakeup occurs. No test in this diff exercises a spurious wakeup scenario (feeding a wakeup without feed_data or feed_eof) to catch this regression.

findings.title: Implicit relative import breaks package import on Python 3
findings.body:
`requests/sessions.py` lives inside the `requests` package, so `adapters` is a sibling submodule, not a top-level module. Under Python 3 (and under `from __future__ import absolute_import` on Python 2) all imports are absolute, so `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` resolves against `sys.path` rather than the package and raises `ImportError: No module named 'adapters'`. Since `sessions` is imported by the package's public surface, this makes `import requests` fail outright rather than failing lazily.

Restore the explicit relative form: `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` (or the fully-qualified `from requests.adapters import HTTPAdapter`). The claim that it is the "same module, cleaner form" only held under Python 2's implicit relative import rules.

findings.title: Implicit relative import lets an arbitrary `adapters` module shadow the package one
findings.body:
`from .adapters import HTTPAdapter` unambiguously resolves to the module inside the `requests` package. `from adapters import HTTPAdapter` does not: under Python 3 (and under Python 2 with `from __future__ import absolute_import`) it is an absolute import resolved against `sys.path`. `sys.path[0]` is the script's directory / current working directory for normal invocations, and `''` for `-c` and interactive use, so any `adapters.py` an attacker can drop into a directory the application is started from — or into any writable `sys.path` entry that precedes the package — is imported and executed instead.

The sink matters here: `HTTPAdapter` is the object that builds the urllib3 `PoolManager` and carries certificate-verification behaviour for every request this `Session` makes. A shadowing module returns an attacker-chosen `HTTPAdapter` whose `send()` can silently disable `verify`, log credentials, or proxy traffic, with no error surfaced to the caller. Arbitrary code also runs at import time.

Independently of the security angle, this import simply fails with `ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'adapters'` on Python 3 in any environment that does not happen to have such a module on the path. Revert to `from .adapters import HTTPAdapter`.

findings.title: get_cookie raises TypeError when request.cookies is None
findings.body:
`HTTPRequest.cookies` is documented and implemented to return `None` when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (`if self._cookies is None: return None`). Dropping the `is not None` check means `name in self.request.cookies` evaluates `in` against `None`, raising `TypeError: argument of type 'NoneType' is not iterable` for any request with a malformed Cookie header — turning a benign "no such cookie" into a 500. Either restore the guard (`if self.request.cookies is not None and name in self.request.cookies:`) or change `HTTPRequest.cookies` to return an empty mapping on parse failure and update its docstring accordingly.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Malformed Cookie header now raises TypeError in get_cookie

findings.title: get_cookie no longer handles None cookies per documented API
findings.body: The `cookies` property on the request object has a documented contract stating it can return None when the Cookie header is present but cannot be parsed (as shown in httpserver.py). The old code checked `if self.request.cookies is not None` to guard against this case. The simplified code removes that check and assumes `cookies` is always a mapping, which will raise TypeError if None. Either restore the guard or update the httpserver.py docstring that promises None is possible.

findings.title: get_cookie docstring may be misleading after cookies becomes nullable
findings.body: If the docstring claim in httpserver.py is accurate—that cookies can be None when the Cookie header cannot be parsed—then the get_cookie docstring 'Gets the value of the cookie with the given name, else default' is incomplete. It does not document that the method will raise an exception (TypeError) if cookies is None rather than returning the default. Update the docstring to clarify behavior when cookies cannot be parsed, or confirm that the httpserver.py docstring is outdated.

findings.title: No test exercises get_cookie when cookies header fails to parse
findings.body: The retrieved httpserver.py shows request.cookies can be None when the Cookie header is present but unparseable, per its own docstring. This diff removes the `self.request.cookies is not None` guard in get_cookie, which would raise TypeError('argument of type NoneType is not iterable') in that case. There is no test in this PR (or apparently in the repo, based on what's shown) exercising get_cookie with a malformed Cookie header, so this behavior change is uncovered.

findings.title: Dropping strip() makes boundary parameter never match
findings.body: `content_type.split(";")` keeps the whitespace that virtually every client emits after the separator, so the second element is `" boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryXYZ"`. With the `.strip()` removed, `partition("=")` yields `k == " boundary"`, which fails the `k == "boundary"` test on line 5, the loop falls through without ever calling `_parse_mime_body`, and the multipart body is silently discarded — all file uploads and form fields vanish with no error. RFC 7231 explicitly permits optional whitespace around parameter separators, so this is not an edge case but the common path. The strip was not redundant: restore `field.strip().partition("=")`, or at minimum strip `k` before comparison (`k.strip() == "boundary"`) and strip `v` so the boundary token has no trailing whitespace.

findings.title: Dropping strip() lets the client control whether multipart bodies are parsed
findings.body:
`content_type.split(";")` leaves the leading space that RFC 7231 permits between parameters, so for the ordinary header `multipart/form-data; boundary=abc` the key is now `" boundary"` and the comparison on line 5 fails; `_parse_mime_body` is never reached and the request's fields and files are silently empty. Conversely `multipart/form-data;boundary=abc` (no space) still parses. The value side is affected too: `v` is no longer right-trimmed, so `boundary=abc ` yields the boundary `"abc "`, which will not match the delimiters in the body.

Entry point: the client-supplied `Content-Type` request header. Sink: the boundary passed to `_parse_mime_body` on line 6 — or, more importantly, the body that now never reaches it.

Beyond the plain correctness break, this gives a remote client a one-character lever over whether Tornado parses a multipart body. Any front-end proxy, WAF or upload scanner that parses the body per spec will see the fields while the application sees none, which is a classic parser-differential bypass; and application code that reads `self.get_argument(...)` for an authorization or CSRF-relevant field will see it missing rather than wrong.

Restore `field.strip().partition("=")`, or strip the key and value individually (`k.strip()`, `v.strip()`), and keep the existing quoted-value handling.

findings.title: No test guards the change to boundary parsing whitespace handling
findings.body: The diff removes `.strip()` before partitioning each Content-Type field into k/v, relying on `k == "boundary"` matching exactly. Since fields after a `;` split typically have a leading space (e.g. `multipart/form-data; boundary=xyz`), `k` would become " boundary" with a leading space, which no longer equals "boundary", silently breaking multipart parsing for the common case. No test in this diff (or referenced) exercises this parsing path with realistic Content-Type headers containing spaces after semicolons, so this regression would not be caught.

findings.title: No test exercises the malformed-port error path
findings.body: The line now reads `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse: %s")` with no `% url` substitution, meaning `%s` is left literally in the string (or raises a TypeError depending on how the exception formats it) whenever a non-digit port is parsed. Nothing in this diff or evidently in the existing suite calls this code path with a malformed port to catch the regression. Add a test that triggers the ValueError/LocationParseError branch by parsing a URL with a non-numeric port and asserts on the resulting message content.

findings.title: Format placeholder left in message after removing the argument
findings.body: The interpolation argument `% url` was removed but the `%s` conversion specifier was left in the string literal. The exception message is now the literal text `Failed to parse: %s`, which is worse than both the original (no URL) and the evidently intended shortened message (stray placeholder that looks like a bug to anyone reading the traceback). If the intent is to drop the detail, drop the placeholder too: `raise LocationParseError("Failed to parse")`. If the URL should be kept, restore `% url`.

findings.title: LocationParseError message no longer includes the URL
findings.body: The error message on line 7 has been shortened to 'Failed to parse: %s', but the format string placeholder is no longer being filled with the URL value. This means the actual error message will be literally 'Failed to parse: %s' rather than 'Failed to parse: <actual-url>', making it unhelpful for debugging. The commit message suggests the detail is in the exception type, but the format string still contains a placeholder that goes unfilled, resulting in misleading output to callers.

findings.title: Unquoted f-string interpolation into shell=True command
findings.body:
`cmd` is built by interpolating caller-supplied `name` and `directory` directly into a string that is then run with `shell=True`. Two concrete consequences:

1. Correctness: any `directory` or `name` containing a space is split into multiple shell words, so `tar` receives the wrong arguments (e.g. `directory="My Photos"` archives `My` and `Photos`). Anything containing `*`, `~`, `$` etc. is silently expanded by the shell.
2. Security: a value such as `directory="x; rm -rf /"` executes arbitrary commands, because the shell parses the whole string.

Fix by dropping the shell and passing an argument list, mirroring `list_exports` on line 5:

```python
return subprocess.run(
    ["tar", "-czf", f"/exports/{name}.tar.gz", directory],
    capture_output=True, check=True,
)
```

Note the list form still lets `name` contain `../`, so validate `name` against a path-component whitelist (or use `os.path.basename`) before joining it into `/exports`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shell command injection in create_archive via name/directory

findings.title: No test coverage for new create_archive function
findings.body: create_archive builds a shell command via string interpolation of `name` and `directory` and executes it with shell=True. There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so neither correct archive creation nor injection-unsafe behavior for malicious `name`/`directory` values would be caught by CI.

findings.title: create_archive returns CompletedProcess while list_exports returns bytes
findings.body: `list_exports` returns `.stdout` (bytes), whereas `create_archive` returns the whole `CompletedProcess` object and does not pass `capture_output=True`, so tar's stderr/stdout go straight to the parent process's streams. Callers of this module will have to special-case each function's return type, and any diagnostic output from a failing tar is lost from the returned value. Consider returning the same shape (or `None`) and capturing output for consistency.

findings.title: Public function `create_archive` lacks documentation
findings.body: The function signature `create_archive(name, directory)` does not indicate to callers that it constructs and executes a shell command, or what constraints exist on the `name` and `directory` parameters. A caller might reasonably pass untrusted input without realizing it will be interpolated directly into a shell command.

findings.title: Wildcard CORS origin combined with credentials: true
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`. This is the canonical cross-origin misconfiguration: it removes origin-based access control from every route the middleware is mounted on, so any site a logged-in user visits can issue credentialed requests to those endpoints and read the responses (session cookies, user data, CSRF tokens) if the browser honours the headers.

Two cases, both bad:
- If the underlying middleware emits a literal `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, browsers reject the credentialed response — so the dashboard feature does not actually work, and the likely next patch is to reflect `req.headers.origin`, which *is* fully exploitable.
- If the middleware (or a proxy/other config) reflects the request origin instead of emitting a literal `*`, the bypass is live today.

Fix: replace the wildcard with an explicit allowlist containing the dashboard origin, mirroring the existing `ALLOWED` value used on line 6, rather than adding a second permissive middleware. Never reflect an arbitrary `Origin` header when `credentials: true`.

findings.title: Wildcard origin with credentials is rejected by browsers
findings.body:
`dashboardCors` sets `origin: "*"` together with `credentials: true`. The `cors` middleware will emit `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` alongside `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`, and the Fetch spec requires user agents to fail any credentialed request whose `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` is the wildcard. The stated purpose of the change — letting the new dashboard call the API with cookies — therefore cannot work: preflights will pass but the actual credentialed responses will be blocked in the browser, and cookies will not be attached.

Reflect the concrete dashboard origin instead, e.g. extend the existing `ALLOWED` list used on line 6 with the dashboard origin, or pass an origin callback/function that echoes the request origin when it is on an allowlist. That also avoids the unrelated problem of advertising credentialed access to every origin.

findings.title: Public CORS config lacks documentation of security model
findings.body: The `dashboardCors` export is a public API whose security contract must be explicitly documented. The combination of `origin: "*"` (accept any origin) and `credentials: true` (send cookies) is a non-standard CORS configuration that violates the CORS specification and creates a security risk. Any caller or reviewer encountering this must understand *why* this configuration exists and what constraints apply to its use. Document the intended dashboard origin, why wildcard is being used, and what security review justified this exception to normal CORS practice.

findings.title: New dashboardCors config has no test coverage
findings.body: The new `dashboardCors` export combines `origin: "*"` with `credentials: true`. Nothing in the diff exercises this config to confirm it behaves as intended (or even that it's a valid combination — most CORS middleware either rejects this or silently disables credentials when origin is a wildcard). No test asserts what headers are actually emitted for a request, so a regression or a broken assumption here would pass silently.

findings.title: Live AcmePay secret key hardcoded in source
findings.body:
`ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is a literal `acme_live_...` credential committed into the repository, replacing the previous `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]` lookup (the `import os` line is deleted). Anyone with read access to the repo, to any clone, to CI logs, or to build artifacts now holds a production payments credential capable of issuing charges and reading account data. Git history makes this permanent even if the line is reverted.

Actions: (1) treat the key as compromised and rotate it in the AcmePay dashboard immediately; (2) restore the environment-variable (or secret-manager) lookup; (3) purge the value from git history, not just from HEAD; (4) consider adding a secret-scanning pre-commit hook so the `acme_live_` prefix is caught next time.

findings.title: Client always uses the live key; env-based configuration is now ignored
findings.body:
`client()` previously resolved the key from `os.environ["ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY"]`, so each environment (dev, CI, staging, prod) supplied its own credential and a missing value raised `KeyError` immediately at call time. After this change the module-level constant on line 4 is a `acme_live_...` key and line 8 assigns it unconditionally, so every environment now authenticates as the production account — test and CI runs that exercise `client()` will issue real charges against live data, and any deployment config that still sets `ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY` is silently ignored rather than erroring.

Restore the environment lookup (or a settings/secret-manager read) so the key varies per environment, and keep the fail-fast behaviour when it is unset.

findings.title: client() behavior change has no test exercising it
findings.body: The client() function changed from reading ACMEPAY_SECRET_KEY from the environment to using a hardcoded module-level constant. Only a fixture file (tests/fixtures/acmepay.py) was added, defining fake_client() and TEST_KEY, but no test actually imports or calls billing.acmepay_client.client() to assert acmepay.api_key is set correctly. Nothing would fail if client() were broken (e.g., wrong key assigned, wrong return value, or import errors).

findings.title: tenant_of() reads tenant_id from an unverified JWT
findings.body:
`tenant_of()` calls `jwt.decode(token, options={"verify_signature": False})` and returns `unverified["tenant_id"]` directly. Signature verification is the only thing binding the claims to your issuer; with it disabled, any caller can craft or edit a bearer token (JWTs are base64, not encrypted) and set `tenant_id` to any value. Anything that scopes a query, a lookup, or a permission decision on this return value will operate on the attacker's chosen tenant — cross-tenant read or write.

The PR description frames this as an optimisation to avoid a round-trip to the key store, but the sibling `claims_for()` on line 7 already does the verified decode with `public_key()` and `algorithms=["RS256"]`. Implement `tenant_of()` on top of it:

```python
def tenant_of(token):
    return claims_for(token)["tenant_id"]
```

If the key fetch is genuinely the cost being avoided, cache `public_key()` (JWKS keys rotate slowly and carry a `kid`) rather than dropping verification. If the unverified decode is only ever meant to pick a key or route before verification, rename it to something like `_unverified_tenant_hint` and never let it reach an authorisation or data-scoping decision.

Note also that `unverified["tenant_id"]` will raise `KeyError` on a token lacking that claim, which is a second, unauthenticated way to trigger a 500.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ tenant_of returns an unverified, attacker-controlled tenant id

findings.title: Public function lacks documentation of unverified signature risk
findings.body: The function `tenant_of()` is a public API that decodes JWT tokens without verifying their signature. A caller unfamiliar with JWT behavior might assume the token has been validated, when in fact it accepts tampered or forged tokens. The contract of this function—that it reads claims without cryptographic verification—must be documented so callers can use it safely in the correct context (e.g., extracting tenant ID before auth, not after).

findings.title: No test for new tenant_of() unverified-decode path
findings.body: tenant_of() is new behavior: it decodes a JWT without verifying its signature and extracts tenant_id. There is no test in this diff exercising it, so nothing would catch a regression (e.g., wrong key name, exception on malformed token, or accidental re-enabling of signature verification) or confirm the intended behavior. Given this reads a security-sensitive claim, at minimum a test should assert that tenant_of returns the correct tenant_id for a token signed with an untrusted/wrong key, and that it raises appropriately on malformed input.

findings.title: Unguarded dict index raises KeyError for tokens without tenant_id
findings.body: A token that decodes successfully but carries no `tenant_id` claim makes line 12 raise `KeyError`, which is unlikely to be handled by callers expecting an auth-layer failure (they would more plausibly catch `jwt` exceptions or get `None`). Since verification is off, an arbitrary well-formed JWT reaches this line, so the case is reachable from untrusted input. Return `unverified.get("tenant_id")` or raise an explicit auth error with a clear message.

findings.title: Missing require_owner check lets any user update any payment method
findings.body:
`update_payment_method` resolves `pm_id` (caller-supplied) straight into `PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)` and then writes `pm.billing_name` and calls `pm.save()` without ever checking ownership. `current_user(request)` is bound to `user` on line 11 but never used — authentication happens, authorisation does not. The read path directly above (line 6) does call `require_owner`, so this is an omission rather than a deliberate policy.

Any signed-in user can enumerate or guess `pm_id` values and rewrite the billing name on another user's stored card. Add `require_owner(user, pm)` immediately after line 12, before any mutation:

```python
user = current_user(request)
pm = PaymentMethod.get(pm_id)
require_owner(user, pm)
pm.billing_name = body["billing_name"]
```

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ update_payment_method mutates object without require_owner check

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ body["billing_name"] raises KeyError on a request missing the field

findings.title: No test coverage for update_payment_method, including missing authz check
findings.body: update_payment_method fetches a PaymentMethod and mutates it without calling require_owner(user, pm), unlike the adjacent read handler which does call it on line 6. No test exists that would catch either the missing ownership check or basic update behavior (e.g., a test asserting a non-owner cannot update another user's payment method, or that billing_name is persisted correctly). As written, any regression or the current authz gap would go undetected.

findings.title: Public function lacks docstring or API contract documentation
findings.body: The `update_payment_method` function is a new public API endpoint but has no docstring documenting its contract, parameters, return value, or authorization model. While the function name is descriptive, callers need to know what fields can be updated, what the body parameter structure should be, and under what circumstances the call will succeed or fail.

findings.title: Rate limit removed from unauthenticated password reset endpoint
findings.body:
`request_reset` is an unauthenticated endpoint that takes a caller-supplied `email` and calls `send_reset_email(email)` with no remaining throttle. Removing `@rate_limit("5/hour")` lets an attacker call it in a loop to (a) mail-bomb an arbitrary victim address, (b) burn the sending domain's reputation and provider quota, causing a denial of service for legitimate resets, and (c) if reset tokens are short-lived or low-entropy, generate an unbounded number of valid tokens for one account, widening the guessing window.

The stated justification — "the email provider already throttles" — does not substitute for this control. Provider-side throttling is applied per sending account/domain, not per requesting IP or per target address, so it caps your own outbound volume (turning the abuse into a self-inflicted outage) rather than preventing per-victim abuse. It also does nothing about the cost of the request path before the send.

Keep a per-IP and per-target-email limiter on this endpoint. If the decorator is being retired in favour of gateway- or middleware-level limiting, that replacement should be visible and asserted by a test before the decorator is dropped.

findings.title: Reset endpoint reports success even when the provider throttles
findings.body: The PR's stated justification is that "the email provider already throttles". With the decorator gone, that provider throttle becomes the only limiter in the path — but `send_reset_email(email)` is called on line 2 with no result check and no exception handling, and line 3 unconditionally returns `{"sent": True}`. So in exactly the scenario the PR relies on (provider rejects or drops the send because it is throttling), the caller is told the email was sent when it was not, and a user who never receives the mail has no signal to retry.
